insufficient_information

The patient does not meet the commercial driver fitness assessment standards due to insufficient information. The patient's blood pressure is within the normal range, but there is no information provided about the patient's antihypertensive therapy or the effectiveness of their treatment. Additionally, there is no information provided about the patient's visual field or diplopia. The patient's hearing assessment is normal, but there is no information provided about the patient's audiometry or the use of hearing aids. The patient has no history of blackouts, but there is no information provided about the patient's blackout risk or the acceptability of that risk. Finally, the patient does not have insulin-treated diabetes, but there is no information provided about the patient's diabetes treatment or the minimization of hypoglycaemia risk.

AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d · section 2.3.1 · PDF 99
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has blood pressure consistently > 170 systolic or > 100 diastolic (treated or untreated). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to annual review, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by the treating specialist* as to whether the following criteria are met: • the person is treated with antihypertensive therapy and effective control of hypertension is achieved over a 4-week follow-up period; and • there are no side effects from the medication that will impair safe driving; and • there is no evidence of damage to target organs relevant to driving. * Ongoing fitness to drive for commercial vehicle drivers may be assessed by the treating GP provided this is mutually agreed by the specialist, GP and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-EXP-896156b1ec73be6c · section 10.2.1 · PDF 214
Commercial • Better eye at least 6/9 • Worse eye at least 6/18 Refer to optomertrist or ophthalmologist for clinical assessment with regard to driving task (also refer to 10.2.1) No No No Yes Not fit to hold an unconditional or conditional licence ditional licence ye at least 6/24 tter eye at least vate With one or both eyes at least 6/12 Commercial • Better eye at least 6/9 • Worse eye at least 6/18 Corrected visual acuity (with glasses)
AFTD2022-EXP-7f3c434bba3c53df · section 4.3 · PDF 120
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Compliance with the standard should be clinically assessed initially. If the initial clinical assessment indicates possible hearing loss, the person should be referred for audiometry. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has unaided hearing loss ≥ 40 dB in the better ear (averaged over the frequencies 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 KHz). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**, as to whether: • the standard is able to be met with a hearing aid***. If the standard is not able to be met with a hearing aid, further individualised assessment should be offered. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account: • the nature of the driving task; and • information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**; and • the results of a practical driver assessment if required. * Stable conditions may not require periodic review. ** Refer to section 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines. *** In some cases, noise amplification as a result of wearing hearing aids may lead to driver distraction and may warrant individualised assessment to determine fitness to drive without the hearing aid (refer to 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines).
AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee · section 1.3 · PDF 71
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Where a person with one or more blackouts of undetermined mechanism does not meet the standards above for a conditional licence but may, in the opinion of the treating specialist, be safe to drive, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority, subject to at least annual review: • if the driver licensing authority, after considering information provided by the treating specialist(s), considers that the risk of a crash caused by a blackout is acceptably low.
AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.

meets_unconditional_standard

The patient meets the unconditional standard for a commercial driver's licence. The patient's blood pressure is within the normal range, and there is no evidence of hypertension. The patient's vision is normal, with uncorrected visual acuity of 6/6 in both eyes. The patient's hearing is normal, with no evidence of hearing loss. There is no history of blackout or diabetes. The patient meets the unconditional standard for a commercial driver's licence.

AFTD2022-EXP-d83c4a25c127adee · section 4.2.2 · PDF 121
The nature of the driving task The driver licensing authority will take into consideration the nature of the driving task as well as the medical condition, particularly when granting a conditional licence. For example, the licence status of a farmer requiring a commercial vehicle licence for the occasional use of a heavy vehicle may be quite different from that of an interstate multiple combination vehicle driver. The examining health professional should bear this in mind when examining a person and when providing advice to the driver licensing authority. Reporting responsibilities Patients should be made aware of the effects of their condition on driving and should be advised of their legal obligation to notify the driver licensing authority where driving is likely to be affected. The health professional may themselves advise the driver licensing authority as the situation requires (refer to section 3.3 and step 6).

Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Compliance with the standard should be clinically assessed initially. If the initial clinical assessment indicates possible hearing loss, the person should be referred for audiometry. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has unaided hearing loss ≥ 40 dB in the better ear (averaged over the frequencies 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 KHz). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**, as to whether: • the standard is able to be met with a hearing aid***. If the standard is not able to be met with a hearing aid, further individualised assessment should be offered. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account: • the nature of the driving task; and • information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**; and • the results of a practical driver assessment if required. * Stable conditions may not require periodic review. ** Refer to section 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines. *** In some cases, noise amplification as a result of wearing hearing aids may lead to driver distraction and may warrant individualised assessment to determine fitness to drive without the hearing aid (refer to 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines).

The nature of the driving task The driver licensing authority will take into consideration the nature of the driving task as well as the medical condition, particularly when granting a conditional licence. For example, the licence status of a farmer requiring a commercial vehicle licence for the occasional use of a heavy vehicle may be quite different from that of an interstate multiple combination vehicle driver. The examining health professional should bear this in mind when examining a person and when providing advice to the driver licensing authority. Reporting responsibilities Patients should be made aware of the effects of their condition on driving and should be advised of their legal obligation to notify the driver licensing authority where driving is likely to be affected. The health professional may themselves advise the driver licensing authority as the situation requires (refer to section 3.3 and step 6).

insufficient_information

The patient's hypertension module is normal, but the guideline evidence suggests that a person with blood pressure consistently > 170 systolic or > 100 diastolic is not fit to hold an unconditional licence. Since the patient's blood pressure is 120/80, this criterion is not met. Additionally, the patient's vision module is normal, but the guideline evidence suggests that a person with unaided hearing loss ≥ 40 dB in the better ear is not fit to hold an unconditional licence. Since the patient's hearing assessment is 'no hearing loss', this criterion is not met. The patient's blackout module is normal, but the guideline evidence suggests that a person with one or more blackouts of undetermined mechanism does not meet the standards for a conditional licence. Since the patient has no blackout history, this criterion is not met. The patient's diabetes module is normal, but the guideline evidence suggests that a person with insulin-treated diabetes is not fit to hold an unconditional licence. Since the patient does not have diabetes, this criterion is not met. However, the patient's modules are not assessed in the context of a conditional licence, as the guideline evidence suggests that a conditional licence may be considered only if the patient meets certain criteria, which are not met in this case.

meets_unconditional_standard

The patient meets the commercial driver fitness assessment standards for all five pilot modules. The patient's blood pressure is within the normal range, and there is no evidence of hypertension. The patient's vision is normal, with uncorrected visual acuity of 6/6 in both eyes. The patient's hearing is normal, with no evidence of hearing loss. There is no history of blackout or undetermined mechanism. The patient does not have diabetes. The patient's overall fitness to drive is deemed satisfactory, and they meet the standards for an unconditional licence.

AFTD2022-EXP-7de596b87146a1f5 · section 2.2.3 · PDF 77
2.2.3. High blood pressure The cut-off blood pressure values at which a person is considered unfit to hold an unconditional licence do not reflect usual goals for managing hypertension. Rather, they reflect levels that are likely to be associated with sudden incapacity due to neurological events (e.g. stroke). The cut-off points are based on expert opinion. It is a general requirement that conditional licences for commercial vehicle drivers are issued by the driver licensing authority based on the advice of an appropriate medical specialist and that these drivers are reviewed periodically by the specialist to determine their ongoing fitness to drive (refer to Part A section 4.4. Conditional licences). In the case of high blood pressure, ongoing fitness to drive may be assessed by the treating general practitioner, provided this is mutually agreed by the specialist and the general practitioner. The initial recommendation of a conditional licence must, however, be based on the opinion of the specialist.

insufficient_information

The patient does not meet the commercial driver fitness assessment standards due to insufficient information. The patient's blood pressure is within the normal range, but there is no information provided about the patient's antihypertensive therapy or the effectiveness of their treatment. Additionally, there is no information provided about the patient's visual field or diplopia. The patient's hearing assessment is normal, but there is no information provided about the patient's audiometry or the use of hearing aids. The patient has no history of blackouts, but there is no information provided about the patient's blackout risk or the acceptability of that risk. Finally, the patient does not have insulin-treated diabetes, but there is no information provided about the patient's diabetes treatment or the minimization of hypoglycaemia risk.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d, AFTD2022-EXP-896156b1ec73be6c, AFTD2022-EXP-7f3c434bba3c53df, AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee, AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461

AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d · section 2.3.1 · PDF 99
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has blood pressure consistently > 170 systolic or > 100 diastolic (treated or untreated). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to annual review, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by the treating specialist* as to whether the following criteria are met: • the person is treated with antihypertensive therapy and effective control of hypertension is achieved over a 4-week follow-up period; and • there are no side effects from the medication that will impair safe driving; and • there is no evidence of damage to target organs relevant to driving. * Ongoing fitness to drive for commercial vehicle drivers may be assessed by the treating GP provided this is mutually agreed by the specialist, GP and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-EXP-896156b1ec73be6c · section 10.2.1 · PDF 214
Commercial • Better eye at least 6/9 • Worse eye at least 6/18 Refer to optomertrist or ophthalmologist for clinical assessment with regard to driving task (also refer to 10.2.1) No No No Yes Not fit to hold an unconditional or conditional licence ditional licence ye at least 6/24 tter eye at least vate With one or both eyes at least 6/12 Commercial • Better eye at least 6/9 • Worse eye at least 6/18 Corrected visual acuity (with glasses)
AFTD2022-EXP-7f3c434bba3c53df · section 4.3 · PDF 120
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Compliance with the standard should be clinically assessed initially. If the initial clinical assessment indicates possible hearing loss, the person should be referred for audiometry. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has unaided hearing loss ≥ 40 dB in the better ear (averaged over the frequencies 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 KHz). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**, as to whether: • the standard is able to be met with a hearing aid***. If the standard is not able to be met with a hearing aid, further individualised assessment should be offered. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account: • the nature of the driving task; and • information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**; and • the results of a practical driver assessment if required. * Stable conditions may not require periodic review. ** Refer to section 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines. *** In some cases, noise amplification as a result of wearing hearing aids may lead to driver distraction and may warrant individualised assessment to determine fitness to drive without the hearing aid (refer to 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines).
AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee · section 1.3 · PDF 71
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Where a person with one or more blackouts of undetermined mechanism does not meet the standards above for a conditional licence but may, in the opinion of the treating specialist, be safe to drive, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority, subject to at least annual review: • if the driver licensing authority, after considering information provided by the treating specialist(s), considers that the risk of a crash caused by a blackout is acceptably low.
AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.

The patient meets the commercial driver fitness assessment standards for all five pilot modules. The patient's blood pressure is within the normal range, and there is no evidence of hypertension. The patient's vision is normal, with uncorrected visual acuity of 6/6 in both eyes. The patient's hearing is normal, with no evidence of hearing loss. There is no history of blackout or undetermined mechanism. The patient does not have diabetes. The patient meets the commercial driver fitness assessment standards for all five pilot modules.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-7de596b87146a1f5, AFTD2022-EXP-896156b1ec73be6c, AFTD2022-HEAR-COM-004, AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee, AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461

AFTD2022-EXP-7de596b87146a1f5 · section 2.2.3 · PDF 77
2.2.3. High blood pressure The cut-off blood pressure values at which a person is considered unfit to hold an unconditional licence do not reflect usual goals for managing hypertension. Rather, they reflect levels that are likely to be associated with sudden incapacity due to neurological events (e.g. stroke). The cut-off points are based on expert opinion. It is a general requirement that conditional licences for commercial vehicle drivers are issued by the driver licensing authority based on the advice of an appropriate medical specialist and that these drivers are reviewed periodically by the specialist to determine their ongoing fitness to drive (refer to Part A section 4.4. Conditional licences). In the case of high blood pressure, ongoing fitness to drive may be assessed by the treating general practitioner, provided this is mutually agreed by the specialist and the general practitioner. The initial recommendation of a conditional licence must, however, be based on the opinion of the specialist.

AFTD2022-EXP-7de596b87146a1f5 · section 2.2.3 · PDF 77
2.2.3. High blood pressure The cut-off blood pressure values at which a person is considered unfit to hold an unconditional licence do not reflect usual goals for managing hypertension. Rather, they reflect levels that are likely to be associated with sudden incapacity due to neurological events (e.g. stroke). The cut-off points are based on expert opinion. It is a general requirement that conditional licences for commercial vehicle drivers are issued by the driver licensing authority based on the advice of an appropriate medical specialist and that these drivers are reviewed periodically by the specialist to determine their ongoing fitness to drive (refer to Part A section 4.4. Conditional licences). In the case of high blood pressure, ongoing fitness to drive may be assessed by the treating general practitioner, provided this is mutually agreed by the specialist and the general practitioner. The initial recommendation of a conditional licence must, however, be based on the opinion of the specialist.

Additionally, there is no information provided about the patient's visual field or diplopia. The patient has no history of blackouts, but there is no information provided about the patient's blackout risk or the acceptability of that risk. Finally, the patient does not have insulin-treated diabetes, but there is no information provided about the patient's diabetes treatment or the minimization of hypoglycaemia risk.

Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has blood pressure consistently > 170 systolic or > 100 diastolic (treated or untreated). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to annual review, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by the treating specialist* as to whether the following criteria are met: • the person is treated with antihypertensive therapy and effective control of hypertension is achieved over a 4-week follow-up period; and • there are no side effects from the medication that will impair safe driving; and • there is no evidence of damage to target organs relevant to driving. * Ongoing fitness to drive for commercial vehicle drivers may be assessed by the treating GP provided this is mutually agreed by the specialist, GP and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.

A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account: • the nature of the driving task; and • information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**; and • the results of a practical driver assessment if required. * Stable conditions may not require periodic review. ** Refer to section 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines. *** In some cases, noise amplification as a result of wearing hearing aids may lead to driver distraction and may warrant individualised assessment to determine fitness to drive without the hearing aid (refer to 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines).

meets_unconditional_standard

The commercial driver assessment indicates that the driver meets the unconditional standard for all five pilot modules. The driver's blood pressure is within the normal range, and there is no evidence of hypertension. The driver's vision is normal, with uncorrected visual acuity of 6/6 in both eyes. The driver's hearing is normal, with no evidence of hearing loss. There is no history of blackout or diabetes. The driver's cardiovascular risk factors are not assessed as part of this pilot program.

Cited: AFTD2022-BLK-COM-006, AFTD2022-EXP-d6142190f29b7662, AFTD2022-EXP-7f3c434bba3c53df, AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d, AFTD2022-EXP-cd83e305301149c8

AFTD2022-BLK-COM-006 · section 1.3 · PDF 69
themselves with the information in this chapter and the tabulated standards before assessing a person’s fitness to drive. Where a firm diagnosis has been made, the standard appropriate to the condition should be referred to in this publication (refer to Figure 6. Management of blackouts and driving). For blackouts due to medical causes not covered in the standard, refer to first principles (refer to Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive – general guidance). For blackouts where, after investigation, it is not possible to diagnose one of the conditions covered elsewhere in this publication, refer to the table for blackouts of uncertain nature over the page.
AFTD2022-EXP-d6142190f29b7662 · section 3.2.3 · PDF 106
Vision Refer to section 10. Vision and eye disorders. Visual acuity should be tested annually. Retinal screening should be undertaken every second year if there is no retinopathy, or more frequently if at high risk. Visual field testing is not required unless clinically indicated.7,8 Neuropathy and foot care While it can be difficult to be prescriptive about neuropathy in the context of driving, it is important that the severity of the condition is assessed. Adequate sensation and movement for the operation of foot controls is required (refer to section 6. Neurological conditions and section 5. Musculoskeletal conditions). Sleep apnoea Sleep apnoea is a common comorbidity affecting many people with type 2 diabetes and has substantial implications for road safety. The treating health professional should be alert to potential signs (e.g. BMI greater than 35) and symptoms, and apply the Epworth Sleepiness Scale as appropriate (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). Cardiovascular There are no diabetes-specific medical standards for cardiovascular risk factors and driver licensing. Consistent with good medical practice, people with diabetes should have their cardiovascular risk factors periodically assessed and treated as required (refer to section 2. Cardiovascular conditions).

AFTD2022-EXP-cd83e305301149c8 · section 10.2.9 · PDF 219
10.2.9. Practical driver assessments A practical driver assessment is not considered to be a safe or reliable method of assessing the effects of disorders of vision on driving, especially the visual fields, because the driver’s response to emergency situations or various environmental conditions cannot be determined. Information about adaptation to visual field defects can be gained from visual field tests such as the Esterman. A practical driver assessment may be helpful in assessing the ability to process visual information (refer to Part A section 2.3.1. Practical driver assessments).

The patient's blood pressure is within the normal range, but there is no information provided about the patient's antihypertensive therapy or the effectiveness of their treatment. Additionally, there is no information provided about the patient's visual field or diplopia. The patient's hearing assessment is normal, but there is no information provided about the patient's audiometry or the use of hearing aids. The patient has no history of blackouts, but there is no information provided about the patient's blackout risk or the acceptability of that risk. Finally, the patient does not have insulin-treated diabetes, but there is no information provided about the patient's diabetes treatment or the minimization of hypoglycaemia risk.

AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d · section 2.3.1 · PDF 99
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has blood pressure consistently > 170 systolic or > 100 diastolic (treated or untreated). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to annual review, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by the treating specialist* as to whether the following criteria are met: • the person is treated with antihypertensive therapy and effective control of hypertension is achieved over a 4-week follow-up period; and • there are no side effects from the medication that will impair safe driving; and • there is no evidence of damage to target organs relevant to driving. * Ongoing fitness to drive for commercial vehicle drivers may be assessed by the treating GP provided this is mutually agreed by the specialist, GP and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.

Commercial • Better eye at least 6/9 • Worse eye at least 6/18 Refer to optomertrist or ophthalmologist for clinical assessment with regard to driving task (also refer to 10.2.1) No No No Yes Not fit to hold an unconditional or conditional licence ditional licence ye at least 6/24 tter eye at least vate With one or both eyes at least 6/12 Commercial • Better eye at least 6/9 • Worse eye at least 6/18 Corrected visual acuity (with glasses)
AFTD2022-EXP-7f3c434bba3c53df · section 4.3 · PDF 120
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Compliance with the standard should be clinically assessed initially. If the initial clinical assessment indicates possible hearing loss, the person should be referred for audiometry. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has unaided hearing loss ≥ 40 dB in the better ear (averaged over the frequencies 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 KHz). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**, as to whether: • the standard is able to be met with a hearing aid***. If the standard is not able to be met with a hearing aid, further individualised assessment should be offered. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account: • the nature of the driving task; and • information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**; and • the results of a practical driver assessment if required. * Stable conditions may not require periodic review. ** Refer to section 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines. *** In some cases, noise amplification as a result of wearing hearing aids may lead to driver distraction and may warrant individualised assessment to determine fitness to drive without the hearing aid (refer to 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines).
AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee · section 1.3 · PDF 71
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Where a person with one or more blackouts of undetermined mechanism does not meet the standards above for a conditional licence but may, in the opinion of the treating specialist, be safe to drive, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority, subject to at least annual review: • if the driver licensing authority, after considering information provided by the treating specialist(s), considers that the risk of a crash caused by a blackout is acceptably low.
AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.

meets_unconditional_standard

The commercial driver assessment indicates that the driver meets the unconditional standard for all five pilot modules. The driver's blood pressure is within the normal range, and there is no evidence of hypertension. The driver's vision is normal, with uncorrected visual acuity of 6/6 in both eyes. The driver's hearing is normal, with no evidence of hearing loss. There is no history of blackout or diabetes. The driver's cardiovascular risk factors are not assessed as part of this pilot program.

Where a firm diagnosis has been made, the standard appropriate to the condition should be referred to in this publication (refer to Figure 6. Management of blackouts and driving). AFTD2022-EXP-d6142190f29b7662 · section 3.2.3 · PDF 106
Vision Refer to section 10. Vision and eye disorders. Visual acuity should be tested annually. Retinal screening should be undertaken every second year if there is no retinopathy, or more frequently if at high risk. Visual field testing is not required unless clinically indicated.7,8 Neuropathy and foot care While it can be difficult to be prescriptive about neuropathy in the context of driving, it is important that the severity of the condition is assessed. Adequate sensation and movement for the operation of foot controls is required (refer to section 6. Neurological conditions and section 5. Musculoskeletal conditions). Sleep apnoea Sleep apnoea is a common comorbidity affecting many people with type 2 diabetes and has substantial implications for road safety. The treating health professional should be alert to potential signs (e.g. BMI greater than 35) and symptoms, and apply the Epworth Sleepiness Scale as appropriate (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). Cardiovascular There are no diabetes-specific medical standards for cardiovascular risk factors and driver licensing. Consistent with good medical practice, people with diabetes should have their cardiovascular risk factors periodically assessed and treated as required (refer to section 2. Cardiovascular conditions).

AFTD2022-EXP-cd83e305301149c8 · section 10.2.9 · PDF 219
10.2.9. Practical driver assessments A practical driver assessment is not considered to be a safe or reliable method of assessing the effects of disorders of vision on driving, especially the visual fields, because the driver’s response to emergency situations or various environmental conditions cannot be determined. Information about adaptation to visual field defects can be gained from visual field tests such as the Esterman. A practical driver assessment may be helpful in assessing the ability to process visual information (refer to Part A section 2.3.1. Practical driver assessments).

hybrid

insufficient_information

The patient's hypertension module is normal, but the guideline evidence suggests that a person with blood pressure consistently > 170 systolic or > 100 diastolic is not fit to hold an unconditional licence. Since the patient's blood pressure is 120/80, this criterion is not met. Additionally, the patient's vision module is normal, but the guideline evidence suggests that a person with unaided hearing loss ≥ 40 dB in the better ear is not fit to hold an unconditional licence. Since the patient's hearing assessment is 'no hearing loss', this criterion is not met. The patient's blackout module is normal, but the guideline evidence suggests that a person with one or more blackouts of undetermined mechanism does not meet the standards for a conditional licence. Since the patient has no blackout history, this criterion is not met. The patient's diabetes module is normal, but the guideline evidence suggests that a person with insulin-treated diabetes is not fit to hold an unconditional licence. Since the patient does not have diabetes, this criterion is not met. However, the patient's modules are not assessed in the context of a conditional licence, as the guideline evidence suggests that a conditional licence may be considered only if the patient meets certain criteria, which are not met in this case.

insufficient_information

The patient does not meet the commercial driver fitness assessment standards due to insufficient information. The patient's blood pressure is within the normal range, but there is no information provided about the patient's antihypertensive therapy or the effectiveness of their treatment. Additionally, there is no information provided about the patient's visual field or diplopia. The patient's hearing assessment is normal, but there is no information provided about the patient's audiometry or the use of hearing aids. The patient has no history of blackouts, but there is no information provided about the patient's blackout risk or the acceptability of that risk. Finally, the patient does not have insulin-treated diabetes, but there is no information provided about the patient's diabetes treatment or the minimization of hypoglycaemia risk.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d, AFTD2022-EXP-896156b1ec73be6c, AFTD2022-EXP-7f3c434bba3c53df, AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee, AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461

AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d · section 2.3.1 · PDF 99
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has blood pressure consistently > 170 systolic or > 100 diastolic (treated or untreated). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to annual review, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by the treating specialist* as to whether the following criteria are met: • the person is treated with antihypertensive therapy and effective control of hypertension is achieved over a 4-week follow-up period; and • there are no side effects from the medication that will impair safe driving; and • there is no evidence of damage to target organs relevant to driving. * Ongoing fitness to drive for commercial vehicle drivers may be assessed by the treating GP provided this is mutually agreed by the specialist, GP and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-EXP-896156b1ec73be6c · section 10.2.1 · PDF 214
Commercial • Better eye at least 6/9 • Worse eye at least 6/18 Refer to optomertrist or ophthalmologist for clinical assessment with regard to driving task (also refer to 10.2.1) No No No Yes Not fit to hold an unconditional or conditional licence ditional licence ye at least 6/24 tter eye at least vate With one or both eyes at least 6/12 Commercial • Better eye at least 6/9 • Worse eye at least 6/18 Corrected visual acuity (with glasses)
AFTD2022-EXP-7f3c434bba3c53df · section 4.3 · PDF 120
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Compliance with the standard should be clinically assessed initially. If the initial clinical assessment indicates possible hearing loss, the person should be referred for audiometry. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has unaided hearing loss ≥ 40 dB in the better ear (averaged over the frequencies 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 KHz). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**, as to whether: • the standard is able to be met with a hearing aid***. If the standard is not able to be met with a hearing aid, further individualised assessment should be offered. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account: • the nature of the driving task; and • information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**; and • the results of a practical driver assessment if required. * Stable conditions may not require periodic review. ** Refer to section 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines. *** In some cases, noise amplification as a result of wearing hearing aids may lead to driver distraction and may warrant individualised assessment to determine fitness to drive without the hearing aid (refer to 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines).
AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee · section 1.3 · PDF 71
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Where a person with one or more blackouts of undetermined mechanism does not meet the standards above for a conditional licence but may, in the opinion of the treating specialist, be safe to drive, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority, subject to at least annual review: • if the driver licensing authority, after considering information provided by the treating specialist(s), considers that the risk of a crash caused by a blackout is acceptably low.
AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.

insufficient_information

The patient's hypertension module is normal, but the guideline evidence suggests that a person with blood pressure consistently > 170 systolic or > 100 diastolic is not fit to hold an unconditional licence. Since the patient's blood pressure is 120/80, this criterion is not met. Additionally, the patient's vision module is normal, but the guideline evidence suggests that a person with unaided hearing loss ≥ 40 dB in the better ear is not fit to hold an unconditional licence. Since the patient's hearing assessment is 'no hearing loss', this criterion is not met. The patient's blackout module is normal, but the guideline evidence suggests that a person with one or more blackouts of undetermined mechanism does not meet the standards for a conditional licence. Since the patient has no blackout history, this criterion is not met. The patient's diabetes module is normal, but the guideline evidence suggests that a person with insulin-treated diabetes is not fit to hold an unconditional licence. Since the patient does not have diabetes, this criterion is not met. However, the patient's modules are not assessed in the context of a conditional licence, as the guideline evidence suggests that a conditional licence may be considered only if the patient meets certain criteria, which are not met in this case.

AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d · section 2.3.1 · PDF 99
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has blood pressure consistently > 170 systolic or > 100 diastolic (treated or untreated). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to annual review, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by the treating specialist* as to whether the following criteria are met: • the person is treated with antihypertensive therapy and effective control of hypertension is achieved over a 4-week follow-up period; and • there are no side effects from the medication that will impair safe driving; and • there is no evidence of damage to target organs relevant to driving. * Ongoing fitness to drive for commercial vehicle drivers may be assessed by the treating GP provided this is mutually agreed by the specialist, GP and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-EXP-896156b1ec73be6c · section 10.2.1 · PDF 214
Commercial • Better eye at least 6/9 • Worse eye at least 6/18 Refer to optomertrist or ophthalmologist for clinical assessment with regard to driving task (also refer to 10.2.1) No No No Yes Not fit to hold an unconditional or conditional licence ditional licence ye at least 6/24 tter eye at least vate With one or both eyes at least 6/12 Commercial • Better eye at least 6/9 • Worse eye at least 6/18 Corrected visual acuity (with glasses)
AFTD2022-EXP-7f3c434bba3c53df · section 4.3 · PDF 120
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Compliance with the standard should be clinically assessed initially. If the initial clinical assessment indicates possible hearing loss, the person should be referred for audiometry. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has unaided hearing loss ≥ 40 dB in the better ear (averaged over the frequencies 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 KHz). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**, as to whether: • the standard is able to be met with a hearing aid***. If the standard is not able to be met with a hearing aid, further individualised assessment should be offered. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account: • the nature of the driving task; and • information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**; and • the results of a practical driver assessment if required. * Stable conditions may not require periodic review. ** Refer to section 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines. *** In some cases, noise amplification as a result of wearing hearing aids may lead to driver distraction and may warrant individualised assessment to determine fitness to drive without the hearing aid (refer to 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines).
AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee · section 1.3 · PDF 71
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Where a person with one or more blackouts of undetermined mechanism does not meet the standards above for a conditional licence but may, in the opinion of the treating specialist, be safe to drive, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority, subject to at least annual review: • if the driver licensing authority, after considering information provided by the treating specialist(s), considers that the risk of a crash caused by a blackout is acceptably low.
AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.

The patient's blood pressure is within the normal range, and there is no evidence of hypertension or any other cardiovascular condition that would impact their ability to drive safely. The patient's vision and hearing are also normal, and there is no indication of any visual or hearing impairment that would affect their ability to drive. Additionally, the patient has no history of blackouts or any other condition that would impact their ability to drive safely. Finally, the patient does not have diabetes, which is not a condition that would impact their ability to drive safely.

AFTD2022-EXP-cd83e305301149c8 · section 10.2.9 · PDF 219
10.2.9. Practical driver assessments A practical driver assessment is not considered to be a safe or reliable method of assessing the effects of disorders of vision on driving, especially the visual fields, because the driver’s response to emergency situations or various environmental conditions cannot be determined. Information about adaptation to visual field defects can be gained from visual field tests such as the Esterman. A practical driver assessment may be helpful in assessing the ability to process visual information (refer to Part A section 2.3.1. Practical driver assessments).

Where a firm diagnosis has been made, the standard appropriate to the condition should be referred to in this publication (refer to Figure 6. Management of blackouts and driving). For blackouts due to medical causes not covered in the standard, refer to first principles (refer to Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive – general guidance). AFTD2022-EXP-d6142190f29b7662 · section 3.2.3 · PDF 106
Vision Refer to section 10. Vision and eye disorders. Visual acuity should be tested annually. Retinal screening should be undertaken every second year if there is no retinopathy, or more frequently if at high risk. Visual field testing is not required unless clinically indicated.7,8 Neuropathy and foot care While it can be difficult to be prescriptive about neuropathy in the context of driving, it is important that the severity of the condition is assessed. Adequate sensation and movement for the operation of foot controls is required (refer to section 6. Neurological conditions and section 5. Musculoskeletal conditions). Sleep apnoea Sleep apnoea is a common comorbidity affecting many people with type 2 diabetes and has substantial implications for road safety. The treating health professional should be alert to potential signs (e.g. BMI greater than 35) and symptoms, and apply the Epworth Sleepiness Scale as appropriate (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). Cardiovascular There are no diabetes-specific medical standards for cardiovascular risk factors and driver licensing. Consistent with good medical practice, people with diabetes should have their cardiovascular risk factors periodically assessed and treated as required (refer to section 2. Cardiovascular conditions).

AFTD2022-EXP-7f3c434bba3c53df · section 4.3 · PDF 120
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Compliance with the standard should be clinically assessed initially. If the initial clinical assessment indicates possible hearing loss, the person should be referred for audiometry. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has unaided hearing loss ≥ 40 dB in the better ear (averaged over the frequencies 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 KHz). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**, as to whether: • the standard is able to be met with a hearing aid***. If the standard is not able to be met with a hearing aid, further individualised assessment should be offered. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account: • the nature of the driving task; and • information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**; and • the results of a practical driver assessment if required. * Stable conditions may not require periodic review. ** Refer to section 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines. *** In some cases, noise amplification as a result of wearing hearing aids may lead to driver distraction and may warrant individualised assessment to determine fitness to drive without the hearing aid (refer to 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines).
AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee · section 1.3 · PDF 71
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Where a person with one or more blackouts of undetermined mechanism does not meet the standards above for a conditional licence but may, in the opinion of the treating specialist, be safe to drive, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority, subject to at least annual review: • if the driver licensing authority, after considering information provided by the treating specialist(s), considers that the risk of a crash caused by a blackout is acceptably low.
AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.

AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d · section 2.3.1 · PDF 99
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has blood pressure consistently > 170 systolic or > 100 diastolic (treated or untreated). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to annual review, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by the treating specialist* as to whether the following criteria are met: • the person is treated with antihypertensive therapy and effective control of hypertension is achieved over a 4-week follow-up period; and • there are no side effects from the medication that will impair safe driving; and • there is no evidence of damage to target organs relevant to driving. * Ongoing fitness to drive for commercial vehicle drivers may be assessed by the treating GP provided this is mutually agreed by the specialist, GP and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-EXP-cd83e305301149c8 · section 10.2.9 · PDF 219
10.2.9. Practical driver assessments A practical driver assessment is not considered to be a safe or reliable method of assessing the effects of disorders of vision on driving, especially the visual fields, because the driver’s response to emergency situations or various environmental conditions cannot be determined. Information about adaptation to visual field defects can be gained from visual field tests such as the Esterman. A practical driver assessment may be helpful in assessing the ability to process visual information (refer to Part A section 2.3.1. Practical driver assessments).

A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account: • the nature of the driving task; and • information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**; and • the results of a practical driver assessment if required. * Stable conditions may not require periodic review. ** Refer to section 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines. *** In some cases, noise amplification as a result of wearing hearing aids may lead to driver distraction and may warrant individualised assessment to determine fitness to drive without the hearing aid (refer to 4.2. Where a firm diagnosis has been made, the standard appropriate to the condition should be referred to in this publication (refer to Figure 6. Management of blackouts and driving). AFTD2022-EXP-d6142190f29b7662 · section 3.2.3 · PDF 106
Vision Refer to section 10. Vision and eye disorders. Visual acuity should be tested annually. Retinal screening should be undertaken every second year if there is no retinopathy, or more frequently if at high risk. Visual field testing is not required unless clinically indicated.7,8 Neuropathy and foot care While it can be difficult to be prescriptive about neuropathy in the context of driving, it is important that the severity of the condition is assessed. Adequate sensation and movement for the operation of foot controls is required (refer to section 6. Neurological conditions and section 5. Musculoskeletal conditions). Sleep apnoea Sleep apnoea is a common comorbidity affecting many people with type 2 diabetes and has substantial implications for road safety. The treating health professional should be alert to potential signs (e.g. BMI greater than 35) and symptoms, and apply the Epworth Sleepiness Scale as appropriate (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). Cardiovascular There are no diabetes-specific medical standards for cardiovascular risk factors and driver licensing. Consistent with good medical practice, people with diabetes should have their cardiovascular risk factors periodically assessed and treated as required (refer to section 2. Cardiovascular conditions).

hybrid

meets_unconditional_standard

The patient meets the criteria for an unconditional commercial driver licence across all assessed modules. Cardiovascular status is normal with blood pressure (120/80) well below the exclusion threshold of >170 systolic or >100 diastolic. Vision is uncorrected at 6/6 in both eyes, exceeding the requirement for the better eye (≥6/9) and worse eye (≥6/18). Hearing loss is absent, meeting the standard of no unaided loss ≥40 dB. No blackouts have occurred, satisfying the requirement that a person with undetermined mechanism blackouts does not meet conditional standards unless risk is deemed acceptably low by a specialist; here, the absence of events implies compliance. Diabetes is not present, avoiding the exclusion for insulin-treated diabetes.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d, AFTD2022-EXP-896156b1ec73be6c, AFTD2022-EXP-7f3c434bba3c53df, AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee, AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461

AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d · section 2.3.1 · PDF 99
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has blood pressure consistently > 170 systolic or > 100 diastolic (treated or untreated). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to annual review, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by the treating specialist* as to whether the following criteria are met: • the person is treated with antihypertensive therapy and effective control of hypertension is achieved over a 4-week follow-up period; and • there are no side effects from the medication that will impair safe driving; and • there is no evidence of damage to target organs relevant to driving. * Ongoing fitness to drive for commercial vehicle drivers may be assessed by the treating GP provided this is mutually agreed by the specialist, GP and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-EXP-896156b1ec73be6c · section 10.2.1 · PDF 214
Commercial • Better eye at least 6/9 • Worse eye at least 6/18 Refer to optomertrist or ophthalmologist for clinical assessment with regard to driving task (also refer to 10.2.1) No No No Yes Not fit to hold an unconditional or conditional licence ditional licence ye at least 6/24 tter eye at least vate With one or both eyes at least 6/12 Commercial • Better eye at least 6/9 • Worse eye at least 6/18 Corrected visual acuity (with glasses)
AFTD2022-EXP-7f3c434bba3c53df · section 4.3 · PDF 120
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Compliance with the standard should be clinically assessed initially. If the initial clinical assessment indicates possible hearing loss, the person should be referred for audiometry. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has unaided hearing loss ≥ 40 dB in the better ear (averaged over the frequencies 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 KHz). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**, as to whether: • the standard is able to be met with a hearing aid***. If the standard is not able to be met with a hearing aid, further individualised assessment should be offered. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account: • the nature of the driving task; and • information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**; and • the results of a practical driver assessment if required. * Stable conditions may not require periodic review. ** Refer to section 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines. *** In some cases, noise amplification as a result of wearing hearing aids may lead to driver distraction and may warrant individualised assessment to determine fitness to drive without the hearing aid (refer to 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines).
AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee · section 1.3 · PDF 71
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Where a person with one or more blackouts of undetermined mechanism does not meet the standards above for a conditional licence but may, in the opinion of the treating specialist, be safe to drive, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority, subject to at least annual review: • if the driver licensing authority, after considering information provided by the treating specialist(s), considers that the risk of a crash caused by a blackout is acceptably low.
AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.

graphrag

temporarily_unfit

The patient is currently unfit to hold a commercial driver's licence due to the presence of hypertension. Although blood pressure readings are within normal limits (120/80 mmHg), verified facts confirm the patient has hypertension, which is an established restrictive criterion under commercial standards requiring treatment and effective control over a 4-week follow-up period before a conditional licence may be considered. The nurse note stating 'Complete normal screening' contradicts the verified fact of hypertension; therefore, the assessment cannot conclude normality based on unverified claims. Vision, hearing, blackout history, and diabetes status are verified as normal or absent, but these do not override the established hypertensive condition.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d, AFTD2022-BLK-COM-002, AFTD2022-DM-COM-002

AFTD2022-BLK-COM-002 · section 1.2.2 · PDF 68
1.2.2. Vasovagal syncope5 The most common cause of transient loss of consciousness is vasovagal syncope (‘fainting’). Where this has been triggered by a well-defined provoking factor or a situation that is unlikely to recur while driving (e.g. prolonged standing, venepuncture or emotional situation), it is not necessary to restrict driving. However, vasovagal syncope may also result from other causes that are not so benign. In such cases, fitness to drive should be assessed according to the cardiovascular conditions standards for syncope (refer to section 2. Cardiovascular conditions).
AFTD2022-DM-COM-002 · section 3.2.1 · PDF 105
Non-driving period after a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ If a severe hypoglycaemic event occurs (as defined in section 3.2.1. Hypoglycaemia), the person should not drive for a significant period of time and will need to be urgently assessed. The minimum period of time before returning to drive is generally six weeks because it often takes many weeks for patterns of glucose control and behaviour to be re-established and for any temporary ‘impaired hypoglycaemia awareness’ to resolve (see below). The non- driving period will depend on factors such as identifying the reason for the episode, the specialist’s opinion and the type of motor vehicle licence. The specialist’s recommendation for returning to driving should be based on the patient’s behaviour and objective measures of glycaemic control (documented blood glucose) over a reasonable interval. Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness 10–14
AFTD2022-EXP-d83c4a25c127adee · section 4.2.2 · PDF 121
The nature of the driving task The driver licensing authority will take into consideration the nature of the driving task as well as the medical condition, particularly when granting a conditional licence. For example, the licence status of a farmer requiring a commercial vehicle licence for the occasional use of a heavy vehicle may be quite different from that of an interstate multiple combination vehicle driver. The examining health professional should bear this in mind when examining a person and when providing advice to the driver licensing authority. Reporting responsibilities Patients should be made aware of the effects of their condition on driving and should be advised of their legal obligation to notify the driver licensing authority where driving is likely to be affected. The health professional may themselves advise the driver licensing authority as the situation requires (refer to section 3.3 and step 6).

Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.

graphrag

temporarily_unfit

The patient is currently unfit to hold a commercial driver's licence due to the presence of hypertension. Although blood pressure readings are within normal limits (120/80 mmHg), verified facts confirm the patient has hypertension, which is an established restrictive criterion under commercial standards requiring treatment and effective control over a 4-week follow-up period before a conditional licence may be considered. The nurse note stating 'Complete normal screening' contradicts the verified fact of hypertension; therefore, the assessment cannot conclude normality based on unverified claims. Vision, hearing, blackout history, and diabetes status are verified as normal or absent, but these do not override the established hypertensive condition.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d, AFTD2022-BLK-COM-002, AFTD2022-DM-COM-002

AFTD2022-BLK-COM-002 · section 1.2.2 · PDF 68
1.2.2. Vasovagal syncope5 The most common cause of transient loss of consciousness is vasovagal syncope (‘fainting’). Where this has been triggered by a well-defined provoking factor or a situation that is unlikely to recur while driving (e.g. prolonged standing, venepuncture or emotional situation), it is not necessary to restrict driving. However, vasovagal syncope may also result from other causes that are not so benign. In such cases, fitness to drive should be assessed according to the cardiovascular conditions standards for syncope (refer to section 2. Cardiovascular conditions).
AFTD2022-DM-COM-002 · section 3.2.1 · PDF 105
Non-driving period after a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ If a severe hypoglycaemic event occurs (as defined in section 3.2.1. Hypoglycaemia), the person should not drive for a significant period of time and will need to be urgently assessed. The minimum period of time before returning to drive is generally six weeks because it often takes many weeks for patterns of glucose control and behaviour to be re-established and for any temporary ‘impaired hypoglycaemia awareness’ to resolve (see below). The non- driving period will depend on factors such as identifying the reason for the episode, the specialist’s opinion and the type of motor vehicle licence. The specialist’s recommendation for returning to driving should be based on the patient’s behaviour and objective measures of glycaemic control (documented blood glucose) over a reasonable interval. Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness 10–14
AFTD2022-EXP-d83c4a25c127adee · section 4.2.2 · PDF 121
The nature of the driving task The driver licensing authority will take into consideration the nature of the driving task as well as the medical condition, particularly when granting a conditional licence. For example, the licence status of a farmer requiring a commercial vehicle licence for the occasional use of a heavy vehicle may be quite different from that of an interstate multiple combination vehicle driver. The examining health professional should bear this in mind when examining a person and when providing advice to the driver licensing authority. Reporting responsibilities Patients should be made aware of the effects of their condition on driving and should be advised of their legal obligation to notify the driver licensing authority where driving is likely to be affected. The health professional may themselves advise the driver licensing authority as the situation requires (refer to section 3.3 and step 6).
AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d · section 2.3.1 · PDF 99
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has blood pressure consistently > 170 systolic or > 100 diastolic (treated or untreated). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to annual review, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by the treating specialist* as to whether the following criteria are met: • the person is treated with antihypertensive therapy and effective control of hypertension is achieved over a 4-week follow-up period; and • there are no side effects from the medication that will impair safe driving; and • there is no evidence of damage to target organs relevant to driving. * Ongoing fitness to drive for commercial vehicle drivers may be assessed by the treating GP provided this is mutually agreed by the specialist, GP and driver licensing authority. hybrid

meets_unconditional_standard

The patient meets the criteria for an unconditional commercial driver licence across all assessed modules. Cardiovascular status is normal with blood pressure (120/80) well below the exclusion threshold of >170 systolic or >100 diastolic. Vision is uncorrected at 6/6 in both eyes, exceeding the requirement for the better eye (≥6/9) and worse eye (≥6/18). Hearing loss is absent, meeting the standard of no unaided loss ≥40 dB. No blackouts have occurred, satisfying the requirement that a person with undetermined mechanism blackouts does not meet conditional standards unless risk is deemed acceptably low by a specialist; here, the absence of events implies compliance. Diabetes is not present, avoiding the exclusion for insulin-treated diabetes.

A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has unaided hearing loss ≥ 40 dB in the better ear (averaged over the frequencies 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 KHz). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**, as to whether: • the standard is able to be met with a hearing aid***. If the standard is not able to be met with a hearing aid, further individualised assessment should be offered. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account: • the nature of the driving task; and • information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**; and • the results of a practical driver assessment if required. * Stable conditions may not require periodic review. ** Refer to section 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines. *** In some cases, noise amplification as a result of wearing hearing aids may lead to driver distraction and may warrant individualised assessment to determine fitness to drive without the hearing aid (refer to 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines).
