hybrid

meets_unconditional_standard

The patient meets the criteria for an unconditional commercial driver licence across all assessed modules. Cardiovascular status is normal with blood pressure (120/80) well below the exclusion threshold of >170 systolic or >100 diastolic. Vision is uncorrected at 6/6 in both eyes, exceeding the requirement for the better eye (≥6/9) and worse eye (≥6/18). Hearing loss is absent, meeting the standard of no unaided loss ≥40 dB. No blackouts have occurred, satisfying the requirement that a person with undetermined mechanism blackouts does not meet conditional standards unless risk is deemed acceptably low by a specialist; here, the absence of events implies compliance. Diabetes is not present, avoiding the exclusion for insulin-treated diabetes.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d, AFTD2022-EXP-896156b1ec73be6c, AFTD2022-EXP-7f3c434bba3c53df, AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee, AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461

AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d · section 2.3.1 · PDF 99
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has blood pressure consistently > 170 systolic or > 100 diastolic (treated or untreated). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to annual review, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by the treating specialist* as to whether the following criteria are met: • the person is treated with antihypertensive therapy and effective control of hypertension is achieved over a 4-week follow-up period; and • there are no side effects from the medication that will impair safe driving; and • there is no evidence of damage to target organs relevant to driving. * Ongoing fitness to drive for commercial vehicle drivers may be assessed by the treating GP provided this is mutually agreed by the specialist, GP and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-EXP-896156b1ec73be6c · section 10.2.1 · PDF 214
Commercial • Better eye at least 6/9 • Worse eye at least 6/18 Refer to optomertrist or ophthalmologist for clinical assessment with regard to driving task (also refer to 10.2.1) No No No Yes Not fit to hold an unconditional or conditional licence ditional licence ye at least 6/24 tter eye at least vate With one or both eyes at least 6/12 Commercial • Better eye at least 6/9 • Worse eye at least 6/18 Corrected visual acuity (with glasses)
AFTD2022-EXP-7f3c434bba3c53df · section 4.3 · PDF 120
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Compliance with the standard should be clinically assessed initially. If the initial clinical assessment indicates possible hearing loss, the person should be referred for audiometry. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has unaided hearing loss ≥ 40 dB in the better ear (averaged over the frequencies 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 KHz). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**, as to whether: • the standard is able to be met with a hearing aid***. If the standard is not able to be met with a hearing aid, further individualised assessment should be offered. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account: • the nature of the driving task; and • information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**; and • the results of a practical driver assessment if required. * Stable conditions may not require periodic review. ** Refer to section 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines. *** In some cases, noise amplification as a result of wearing hearing aids may lead to driver distraction and may warrant individualised assessment to determine fitness to drive without the hearing aid (refer to 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines).
AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee · section 1.3 · PDF 71
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Where a person with one or more blackouts of undetermined mechanism does not meet the standards above for a conditional licence but may, in the opinion of the treating specialist, be safe to drive, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority, subject to at least annual review: • if the driver licensing authority, after considering information provided by the treating specialist(s), considers that the risk of a crash caused by a blackout is acceptably low.
AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.

insufficient_information

The nurse_note indicates a 'Complete normal screening' and provides specific values for blood pressure, vision (right and left), hearing, blackout status, and diabetes presence. However, the verified_patient_facts only contain data for cardiovascular blood pressure and uncorrected vision metrics. The fields for hearing ('hearing.clinical_assessment'), blackout ('blackout.occurred'), and diabetes ('diabetes.present') are mentioned in the nurse_note but are absent from verified_patient_facts. Per the instructions, fields absent from verified_patient_facts remain unverified; an unverified negative finding cannot be declared normal. Furthermore, guideline_evidence is empty, preventing the establishment of any licensing standards or criteria against which to measure these findings. Consequently, no established restrictive criterion can be confirmed, and unresolved modules (hearing, blackout, diabetes) cannot be assessed as normal due to lack of verified data.

hybrid

meets_unconditional_standard

The patient meets the criteria for an unconditional commercial driver licence across all assessed modules. Cardiovascular status is normal with blood pressure (120/80) well below the exclusion threshold of >170 systolic or >100 diastolic. Vision is uncorrected at 6/6 in both eyes, exceeding the requirement for the better eye (≥6/9) and worse eye (≥6/18). Hearing loss is absent, meeting the standard of no unaided loss ≥40 dB. No blackouts have occurred, satisfying the requirement that a person with undetermined mechanism blackouts does not meet conditional standards unless risk is deemed acceptably low by a specialist; here, the absence of events implies compliance. Diabetes is not present, avoiding the exclusion for insulin-treated diabetes.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-f57fef6c660a1e6d, AFTD2022-EXP-896156b1ec73be6c, AFTD2022-EXP-7f3c434bba3c53df, AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee, AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461

Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has blood pressure consistently > 170 systolic or > 100 diastolic (treated or untreated). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to annual review, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by the treating specialist* as to whether the following criteria are met: • the person is treated with antihypertensive therapy and effective control of hypertension is achieved over a 4-week follow-up period; and • there are no side effects from the medication that will impair safe driving; and • there is no evidence of damage to target organs relevant to driving. * Ongoing fitness to drive for commercial vehicle drivers may be assessed by the treating GP provided this is mutually agreed by the specialist, GP and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.

Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Compliance with the standard should be clinically assessed initially. If the initial clinical assessment indicates possible hearing loss, the person should be referred for audiometry. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has unaided hearing loss ≥ 40 dB in the better ear (averaged over the frequencies 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 KHz). A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account the nature of the driving task and information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**, as to whether: • the standard is able to be met with a hearing aid***. If the standard is not able to be met with a hearing aid, further individualised assessment should be offered. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review*, taking into account: • the nature of the driving task; and • information provided by an ENT specialist or audiologist**; and • the results of a practical driver assessment if required. * Stable conditions may not require periodic review. ** Refer to section 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines. *** In some cases, noise amplification as a result of wearing hearing aids may lead to driver distraction and may warrant individualised assessment to determine fitness to drive without the hearing aid (refer to 4.2. General assessment and management guidelines).

no_evidence

insufficient_information

The nurse_note indicates a 'Complete normal screening' and provides specific values for blood pressure, vision (right and left), hearing, blackout status, and diabetes presence. However, the verified_patient_facts only contain data for cardiovascular blood pressure and uncorrected vision metrics. The fields for hearing ('hearing.clinical_assessment'), blackout ('blackout.occurred'), and diabetes ('diabetes.present') are mentioned in the nurse_note but are absent from verified_patient_facts. Per the instructions, fields absent from verified_patient_facts remain unverified; an unverified negative finding cannot be declared normal. Furthermore, guideline_evidence is empty, preventing the establishment of any licensing standards or criteria against which to measure these findings. Consequently, no established restrictive criterion can be confirmed, and unresolved modules (hearing, blackout, diabetes) cannot be assessed as normal due to lack of verified data.

hybrid

insufficient_information

The patient has reported a blackout (verified: blackout.occurred = true), but the mechanism remains undetermined (verified: blackout.mechanism_status = 'under_investigation'). According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02, a person should not drive for 5 years following a single blackout of undetermined nature. Furthermore, without an established diagnosis (e.g., syncope, seizure) or confirmation that the mechanism is not covered by standards, no conditional licence criteria can be met. The nurse note indicates the investigation is ongoing; therefore, the specific restrictive criterion regarding the duration of abstinence cannot be established as satisfied, nor can a safe-to-drive conclusion be drawn without specialist input on treatability and recurrence likelihood (AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01). Other modules (BP, vision, hearing, diabetes) are verified but do not override the undetermined blackout status.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02, AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01, AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0

AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01 · section 1.2.3 · PDF 68
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical causes not covered in the standards If the cause of the blackout is determined to be a medical condition not covered in the standards, then first principles regarding fitness to drive should be applied (refer to Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive – general guidance). Considerations include the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and the treatability of the condition as well as the nature of the driving task. There should also be an appropriate review period. A more stringent approach should be considered for commercial vehicle drivers.
AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02 · section 1.3 · PDF 70
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person should not drive for 5 years following a single blackout of undetermined nature. A person should not drive for 10 years following two or more blackouts of undetermined nature separated by a 24- hour period. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has experienced blackouts that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, seizure or another condition. If there has been a single blackout or more than one blackout within a 24-hour period, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into account information provided by an appropriate specialist as to whether the following criterion is met: • there have been no further blackouts for at least 5 years. If there have been two or more blackouts separated by at least 24 hours, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into account information provided by an appropriate specialist as to whether the following criterion is met: • there have been no further blackouts for at least 10 years.

temporarily_unfit

The patient has reported an occurrence of blackout (verified fact: blackout.occurred = true). However, the mechanism of this blackout remains undetermined as it is currently under investigation (verified fact: blackout.mechanism_status = 'under_investigation'). According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0 and AFTD2022-EXP-05643c50d6cf5973, fitness to drive should not be assessed until the mechanism is ascertained. Furthermore, guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-05643c50d6cf5973 explicitly advises that people should not drive until the mechanism is ascertained and the corresponding standard met. While other modules (cardiovascular, vision, hearing) are within normal limits or unverified but not negative, the unresolved nature of the blackout prevents establishing a conditional licence qualification.

hybrid

insufficient_information

The patient has reported a blackout (verified: blackout.occurred = true), but the mechanism remains undetermined (verified: blackout.mechanism_status = 'under_investigation'). According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02, a person should not drive for 5 years following a single blackout of undetermined nature. Furthermore, without an established diagnosis (e.g., syncope, seizure) or confirmation that the mechanism is not covered by standards, no conditional licence criteria can be met. The nurse note indicates the investigation is ongoing; therefore, the specific restrictive criterion regarding the duration of abstinence cannot be established as satisfied, nor can a safe-to-drive conclusion be drawn without specialist input on treatability and recurrence likelihood (AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01). Other modules (BP, vision, hearing, diabetes) are verified but do not override the undetermined blackout status.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02, AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01, AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0

AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01 · section 1.2.3 · PDF 68
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical causes not covered in the standards If the cause of the blackout is determined to be a medical condition not covered in the standards, then first principles regarding fitness to drive should be applied (refer to Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive – general guidance). Considerations include the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and the treatability of the condition as well as the nature of the driving task. There should also be an appropriate review period. A more stringent approach should be considered for commercial vehicle drivers.
AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02 · section 1.3 · PDF 70
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person should not drive for 5 years following a single blackout of undetermined nature. A person should not drive for 10 years following two or more blackouts of undetermined nature separated by a 24- hour period. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has experienced blackouts that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, seizure or another condition. If there has been a single blackout or more than one blackout within a 24-hour period, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into account information provided by an appropriate specialist as to whether the following criterion is met: • there have been no further blackouts for at least 5 years. If there have been two or more blackouts separated by at least 24 hours, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into account information provided by an appropriate specialist as to whether the following criterion is met: • there have been no further blackouts for at least 10 years.
AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee · section 1.3 · PDF 71
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Where a person with one or more blackouts of undetermined mechanism does not meet the standards above for a conditional licence but may, in the opinion of the treating specialist, be safe to drive, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority, subject to at least annual review: • if the driver licensing authority, after considering information provided by the treating specialist(s), considers that the risk of a crash caused by a blackout is acceptably low.
AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0 · section 1.2.4 · PDF 69
1.2.4. Blackouts of undetermined mechanism If, despite extensive investigation, the mechanism of a blackout cannot be determined, fitness to drive should be assessed according to section 1.3. Medical standards for licensing. The standards for blackout of undetermined mechanism are similar to those for seizure.
AFTD2022-EXP-05643c50d6cf5973 · section 1.2.1 · PDF 68
cardiovascular and neurological investigations and referral to several specialists. People should be advised not to drive until the mechanism is ascertained and the corresponding standard met. Some drivers may attribute a crash or driving mishap to a ‘blackout’ to excuse an event that occurred for some other reason such as inattention or distraction (e.g. a mobile phone conversation). There will also be a small proportion of cases in which a clear cause cannot be established.

insufficient_information

The patient has reported a blackout (verified: blackout.occurred = true), but the mechanism remains undetermined (verified: blackout.mechanism_status = 'under_investigation'). According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02, a person should not drive for 5 years following a single blackout of undetermined nature. Furthermore, without an established diagnosis (e.g., syncope, seizure) or confirmation that the mechanism is not covered by standards, no conditional licence criteria can be met. The nurse note indicates the investigation is ongoing; therefore, the specific restrictive criterion regarding the duration of abstinence cannot be established as satisfied, nor can a safe-to-drive conclusion be drawn without specialist input on treatability and recurrence likelihood (AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01). Other modules (BP, vision, hearing, diabetes) are verified but do not override the undetermined blackout status.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02, AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01, AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0

AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01 · section 1.2.3 · PDF 68
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical causes not covered in the standards If the cause of the blackout is determined to be a medical condition not covered in the standards, then first principles regarding fitness to drive should be applied (refer to Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive – general guidance). Considerations include the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and the treatability of the condition as well as the nature of the driving task. There should also be an appropriate review period. A more stringent approach should be considered for commercial vehicle drivers.
AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02 · section 1.3 · PDF 70
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person should not drive for 5 years following a single blackout of undetermined nature. A person should not drive for 10 years following two or more blackouts of undetermined nature separated by a 24- hour period. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has experienced blackouts that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, seizure or another condition. If there has been a single blackout or more than one blackout within a 24-hour period, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into account information provided by an appropriate specialist as to whether the following criterion is met: • there have been no further blackouts for at least 5 years. If there have been two or more blackouts separated by at least 24 hours, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into account information provided by an appropriate specialist as to whether the following criterion is met: • there have been no further blackouts for at least 10 years.
AFTD2022-EXP-5546204ae4ffe0ee · section 1.3 · PDF 71
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) Where a person with one or more blackouts of undetermined mechanism does not meet the standards above for a conditional licence but may, in the opinion of the treating specialist, be safe to drive, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority, subject to at least annual review: • if the driver licensing authority, after considering information provided by the treating specialist(s), considers that the risk of a crash caused by a blackout is acceptably low.
AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0 · section 1.2.4 · PDF 69
1.2.4. Blackouts of undetermined mechanism If, despite extensive investigation, the mechanism of a blackout cannot be determined, fitness to drive should be assessed according to section 1.3. Medical standards for licensing. The standards for blackout of undetermined mechanism are similar to those for seizure.
AFTD2022-EXP-05643c50d6cf5973 · section 1.2.1 · PDF 68
cardiovascular and neurological investigations and referral to several specialists. People should be advised not to drive until the mechanism is ascertained and the corresponding standard met. Some drivers may attribute a crash or driving mishap to a ‘blackout’ to excuse an event that occurred for some other reason such as inattention or distraction (e.g. a mobile phone conversation). There will also be a small proportion of cases in which a clear cause cannot be established.

insufficient_information

The patient has reported a blackout (verified: blackout.occurred = true), but the mechanism remains undetermined (verified: blackout.mechanism_status = 'under_investigation'). According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02, a person should not drive for 5 years following a single blackout of undetermined nature. Furthermore, without an established diagnosis (e.g., syncope, seizure) or confirmation that the mechanism is not covered by standards, no conditional licence criteria can be met. The nurse note indicates the investigation is ongoing; therefore, the specific restrictive criterion regarding the duration of abstinence cannot be established as satisfied, nor can a safe-to-drive conclusion be drawn without specialist input on treatability and recurrence likelihood (AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01). Other modules (BP, vision, hearing, diabetes) are verified but do not override the undetermined blackout status.

AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01 · section 1.2.3 · PDF 68
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical causes not covered in the standards If the cause of the blackout is determined to be a medical condition not covered in the standards, then first principles regarding fitness to drive should be applied (refer to Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive – general guidance). Considerations include the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and the treatability of the condition as well as the nature of the driving task. There should also be an appropriate review period. A more stringent approach should be considered for commercial vehicle drivers.
AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02 · section 1.3 · PDF 70
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person should not drive for 5 years following a single blackout of undetermined nature. A person should not drive for 10 years following two or more blackouts of undetermined nature separated by a 24- hour period. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has experienced blackouts that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, seizure or another condition. If there has been a single blackout or more than one blackout within a 24-hour period, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into account information provided by an appropriate specialist as to whether the following criterion is met: • there have been no further blackouts for at least 5 years. If there have been two or more blackouts separated by at least 24 hours, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into account information provided by an appropriate specialist as to whether the following criterion is met: • there have been no further blackouts for at least 10 years.

insufficient_information

The patient has experienced a blackout diagnosed as hypoglycaemia (verified_patient_facts: blackout.diagnosis = 'hypoglycaemia', diabetes.present = false). However, the provided guideline evidence does not contain specific licensing standards or exclusion criteria for blackouts caused by hypoglycaemia. The guidelines only address blackouts of 'undetermined nature' (AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d55576d02) or medical causes 'not covered in the standards' (AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01). Without a specific guideline entry for hypoglycaemia, it is not possible to establish whether this condition meets conditional licence requirements or if an exclusion applies. Therefore, no established restrictive criterion can be confirmed, and the assessment cannot proceed to determine fitness based on the supplied evidence.

temporarily_unfit

The patient has a confirmed history of blackout (verified_patient_facts: blackout.occurred = true) diagnosed as hypoglycaemia (verified_patient_facts: blackout.diagnosis = 'hypoglycaemia'). According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-BLK-COM-006, where a firm diagnosis has been made, the standard appropriate to the condition should be referred to. However, verified_patient_facts confirms diabetes is absent (diabetes.present = false). Hypoglycaemia in the absence of diagnosed diabetes requires investigation into other metabolic causes or triggers. Guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0 states that if the mechanism cannot be determined, fitness is assessed similarly to seizures; however, here a diagnosis exists but lacks specific licensing standard coverage in the provided text for non-diabetic hypoglycaemia. Guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01 applies first principles for conditions not covered in standards, noting that for commercial drivers a more stringent approach is required and an appropriate review period must be considered. Since no specific standard for non-diabetic hypoglycaemia blackout is provided to declare fitness, the established restrictive criterion (history of blackout with unverified metabolic context) prevents a fit declaration.

The patient has experienced a blackout diagnosed as hypoglycaemia (verified_patient_facts: blackout.diagnosis = 'hypoglycaemia', diabetes.present = false). However, the provided guideline evidence does not contain specific licensing standards or exclusion criteria for blackouts caused by hypoglycaemia. The guidelines only address blackouts of 'undetermined nature' (AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d55576d02) or medical causes 'not covered in the standards' (AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01). Without a specific guideline entry for hypoglycaemia, it is not possible to establish whether this condition meets conditional licence requirements or if an exclusion applies. Therefore, no established restrictive criterion can be confirmed, and the assessment cannot proceed to determine fitness based on the supplied evidence.

Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person should not drive for 5 years following a single blackout of undetermined nature. A person should not drive for 10 years following two or more blackouts of undetermined nature separated by a 24- hour period. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has experienced blackouts that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, seizure or another condition. If there has been a single blackout or more than one blackout within a 24-hour period, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into account information provided by an appropriate specialist as to whether the following criterion is met: • there have been no further blackouts for at least 5 years. If there have been two or more blackouts separated by at least 24 hours, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into account information provided by an appropriate specialist as to whether the following criterion is met: • there have been no further blackouts for at least 10 years.

insufficient_information

The patient has experienced a blackout diagnosed as hypoglycaemia (verified_patient_facts: blackout.diagnosis = 'hypoglycaemia', diabetes.present = false). However, the provided guideline evidence does not contain specific licensing standards or exclusion criteria for blackouts caused by hypoglycaemia. The guidelines only address blackouts of 'undetermined nature' (AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d55576d02) or medical causes 'not covered in the standards' (AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01). Without a specific guideline entry for hypoglycaemia, it is not possible to establish whether this condition meets conditional licence requirements or if an exclusion applies. Therefore, no established restrictive criterion can be confirmed, and the assessment cannot proceed to determine fitness based on the supplied evidence.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-fc1ed73935da2203, AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01, AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02

AFTD2022-EXP-fc1ed73935da2203 · section 1.2.1 · PDF 68
1.2.1. General considerations1–4 Blackouts may occur due to a range of mechanisms including: • vasovagal syncope or ‘faint’, which accounts for more than 50 per cent of blackouts and may be due to factors such as hot weather, emotion or venepuncture but may also be due to more serious causes that may recur • syncope due to other cardiovascular causes such as structural heart disease, arrhythmias or vascular disease • epileptic seizure, which accounts for less than 10 per cent of blackouts • other causes including metabolic causes (e.g. hypoglycaemia), drug intoxication or a sleep disorder. Determination of the mechanism of a blackout may be straightforward based on history, investigations and specialist referral, and the person may be managed as per the appropriate chapter. Alternatively, it may require extensive
AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01 · section 1.2.3 · PDF 68
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical causes not covered in the standards If the cause of the blackout is determined to be a medical condition not covered in the standards, then first principles regarding fitness to drive should be applied (refer to Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive – general guidance). Considerations include the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and the treatability of the condition as well as the nature of the driving task. There should also be an appropriate review period. A more stringent approach should be considered for commercial vehicle drivers.
AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02 · section 1.3 · PDF 70
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person should not drive for 5 years following a single blackout of undetermined nature. A person should not drive for 10 years following two or more blackouts of undetermined nature separated by a 24- hour period. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has experienced blackouts that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, seizure or another condition. If there has been a single blackout or more than one blackout within a 24-hour period, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into account information provided by an appropriate specialist as to whether the following criterion is met: • there have been no further blackouts for at least 5 years. If there have been two or more blackouts separated by at least 24 hours, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into account information provided by an appropriate specialist as to whether the following criterion is met: • there have been no further blackouts for at least 10 years.
AFTD2022-EXP-05643c50d6cf5973 · section 1.2.1 · PDF 68
cardiovascular and neurological investigations and referral to several specialists. People should be advised not to drive until the mechanism is ascertained and the corresponding standard met. Some drivers may attribute a crash or driving mishap to a ‘blackout’ to excuse an event that occurred for some other reason such as inattention or distraction (e.g. a mobile phone conversation). There will also be a small proportion of cases in which a clear cause cannot be established.
AFTD2022-BLK-COM-006 · section 1.3 · PDF 69
themselves with the information in this chapter and the tabulated standards before assessing a person’s fitness to drive. Where a firm diagnosis has been made, the standard appropriate to the condition should be referred to in this publication (refer to Figure 6. Management of blackouts and driving). For blackouts due to medical causes not covered in the standard, refer to first principles (refer to Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive – general guidance). For blackouts where, after investigation, it is not possible to diagnose one of the conditions covered elsewhere in this publication, refer to the table for blackouts of uncertain nature over the page.

temporarily_unfit

The patient has a confirmed history of blackout (verified_patient_facts: blackout.occurred = true) diagnosed as hypoglycaemia (verified_patient_facts: blackout.diagnosis = 'hypoglycaemia'). According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-BLK-COM-006, where a firm diagnosis has been made, the standard appropriate to the condition should be referred to. However, verified_patient_facts confirms diabetes is absent (diabetes.present = false). Hypoglycaemia in the absence of diagnosed diabetes requires investigation into other metabolic causes or triggers. Guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0 states that if the mechanism cannot be determined, fitness is assessed similarly to seizures; however, here a diagnosis exists but lacks specific licensing standard coverage in the provided text for non-diabetic hypoglycaemia. Guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01 applies first principles for conditions not covered in standards, noting that for commercial drivers a more stringent approach is required and an appropriate review period must be considered. Since no specific standard for non-diabetic hypoglycaemia blackout is provided to declare fitness, the established restrictive criterion (history of blackout with unverified metabolic context) prevents a fit declaration.

insufficient_information

The patient has experienced a blackout diagnosed as hypoglycaemia (verified_patient_facts: blackout.diagnosis = 'hypoglycaemia', diabetes.present = false). However, the provided guideline evidence does not contain specific licensing standards or exclusion criteria for blackouts caused by hypoglycaemia. The guidelines only address blackouts of 'undetermined nature' (AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d55576d02) or medical causes 'not covered in the standards' (AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01). Without a specific guideline entry for hypoglycaemia, it is not possible to establish whether this condition meets conditional licence requirements or if an exclusion applies. Therefore, no established restrictive criterion can be confirmed, and the assessment cannot proceed to determine fitness based on the supplied evidence.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-fc1ed73935da2203, AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01, AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02

AFTD2022-EXP-fc1ed73935da2203 · section 1.2.1 · PDF 68
1.2.1. General considerations1–4 Blackouts may occur due to a range of mechanisms including: • vasovagal syncope or ‘faint’, which accounts for more than 50 per cent of blackouts and may be due to factors such as hot weather, emotion or venepuncture but may also be due to more serious causes that may recur • syncope due to other cardiovascular causes such as structural heart disease, arrhythmias or vascular disease • epileptic seizure, which accounts for less than 10 per cent of blackouts • other causes including metabolic causes (e.g. hypoglycaemia), drug intoxication or a sleep disorder. Determination of the mechanism of a blackout may be straightforward based on history, investigations and specialist referral, and the person may be managed as per the appropriate chapter. Alternatively, it may require extensive
AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01 · section 1.2.3 · PDF 68
1.2.3. Blackouts due to medical causes not covered in the standards If the cause of the blackout is determined to be a medical condition not covered in the standards, then first principles regarding fitness to drive should be applied (refer to Part A section 2. Assessing fitness to drive – general guidance). Considerations include the likelihood of recurrence of blackout and the treatability of the condition as well as the nature of the driving task. There should also be an appropriate review period. A more stringent approach should be considered for commercial vehicle drivers.
AFTD2022-EXP-bbf242d555576d02 · section 1.3 · PDF 70
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person should not drive for 5 years following a single blackout of undetermined nature. A person should not drive for 10 years following two or more blackouts of undetermined nature separated by a 24- hour period. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has experienced blackouts that cannot be diagnosed as syncope, seizure or another condition. If there has been a single blackout or more than one blackout within a 24-hour period, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into account information provided by an appropriate specialist as to whether the following criterion is met: • there have been no further blackouts for at least 5 years. If there have been two or more blackouts separated by at least 24 hours, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into account information provided by an appropriate specialist as to whether the following criterion is met: • there have been no further blackouts for at least 10 years.
AFTD2022-EXP-05643c50d6cf5973 · section 1.2.1 · PDF 68
cardiovascular and neurological investigations and referral to several specialists. People should be advised not to drive until the mechanism is ascertained and the corresponding standard met. Some drivers may attribute a crash or driving mishap to a ‘blackout’ to excuse an event that occurred for some other reason such as inattention or distraction (e.g. a mobile phone conversation). There will also be a small proportion of cases in which a clear cause cannot be established.

themselves with the information in this chapter and the tabulated standards before assessing a person’s fitness to drive. For blackouts where, after investigation, it is not possible to diagnose one of the conditions covered elsewhere in this publication, refer to the table for blackouts of uncertain nature over the page.

temporarily_unfit

The patient has a confirmed history of blackout (verified_patient_facts: blackout.occurred = true) diagnosed as hypoglycaemia (verified_patient_facts: blackout.diagnosis = 'hypoglycaemia'). According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-BLK-COM-006, where a firm diagnosis has been made, the standard appropriate to the condition should be referred to. However, verified_patient_facts confirms diabetes is absent (diabetes.present = false). Hypoglycaemia in the absence of diagnosed diabetes requires investigation into other metabolic causes or triggers. Guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0 states that if the mechanism cannot be determined, fitness is assessed similarly to seizures; however, here a diagnosis exists but lacks specific licensing standard coverage in the provided text for non-diabetic hypoglycaemia. Guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01 applies first principles for conditions not covered in standards, noting that for commercial drivers a more stringent approach is required and an appropriate review period must be considered. Since no specific standard for non-diabetic hypoglycaemia blackout is provided to declare fitness, the established restrictive criterion (history of blackout with unverified metabolic context) prevents a fit declaration.

If there have been two or more blackouts separated by at least 24 hours, a conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into account information provided by an appropriate specialist as to whether the following criterion is met: • there have been no further blackouts for at least 10 years.

temporarily_unfit

The patient has a confirmed history of blackout (verified_patient_facts: blackout.occurred = true) diagnosed as hypoglycaemia (verified_patient_facts: blackout.diagnosis = 'hypoglycaemia'). According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-BLK-COM-006, where a firm diagnosis has been made, the standard appropriate to the condition should be referred to. However, verified_patient_facts confirms diabetes is absent (diabetes.present = false). Hypoglycaemia in the absence of diagnosed diabetes requires investigation into other metabolic causes or triggers. Guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-3a8e08652c83a2d0 states that if the mechanism cannot be determined, fitness is assessed similarly to seizures; however, here a diagnosis exists but lacks specific licensing standard coverage in the provided text for non-diabetic hypoglycaemia. Guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-2332d9548f2abd01 applies first principles for conditions not covered in standards, noting that for commercial drivers a more stringent approach is required and an appropriate review period must be considered. Since no specific standard for non-diabetic hypoglycaemia blackout is provided to declare fitness, the established restrictive criterion (history of blackout with unverified metabolic context) prevents a fit declaration.

General considerations1–4 Blackouts may occur due to a range of mechanisms including: • vasovagal syncope or ‘faint’, which accounts for more than 50 per cent of blackouts and may be due to factors such as hot weather, emotion or venepuncture but may also be due to more serious causes that may recur • syncope due to other cardiovascular causes such as structural heart disease, arrhythmias or vascular disease • epileptic seizure, which accounts for less than 10 per cent of blackouts • other causes including metabolic causes (e.g. hypoglycaemia), drug intoxication or a sleep disorder. Determination of the mechanism of a blackout may be straightforward based on history, investigations and specialist referral, and the person may be managed as per the appropriate chapter. meets_unconditional_standard

The patient has diabetes present but is not insulin-treated, as the treatment category is 'diet_and_exercise_only'. According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27 (section 3.3), a person with non-insulin treated diabetes mellitus may drive without licence restriction. The patient meets all criteria for an unconditional licence: no recent severe hypoglycaemic events (verified_patient_facts blackout.occurred = false, diabetes.severe_hypoglycaemic_event.occurred = false), treatment regimen minimises hypoglycaemia risk (verified_patient_facts diabetes.regimen_minimises_hypoglycaemia = true), early warning symptoms are present (verified_patient_facts diabetes.hypoglycaemia_awareness = true), and there are no driving-relevant end-organ effects (verified_patient_facts diabetes.driving_relevant_end_organ_effects = false). Vision is within normal limits (verified_patient_facts vision.uncorrected.right.snellen = '6/6', etc.), and cardiovascular blood pressure is stable (120/80 mmHg), though specific licensing standards for these parameters are not explicitly defined in the provided guidelines, they do not constitute a disqualifying finding based on the available evidence.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461, AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27

AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27 · section 3.3 · PDF 112
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person with diabetes treated by diet and exercise alone may drive without licence restriction. They should he reviewed by their treating doctor periodically regarding the progression of their diabetes. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has non–insulin treated diabetes mellitus and is being treated with glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes* on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • there is an absence of end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication. * For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes who is being treated with metformin alone, the annual review for a conditional licence may be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, specialist and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-EXP-bfabe371c5d42229 · section 3.2.3 · PDF 106
3.2.3. Comorbidities and end-organ complications1–3,8,9 Assessment and management of comorbidities is an important aspect of managing people with diabetes with respect to their fitness to drive. This should be part of routine review as per recommended practice and may include, but is not limited to, the following.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-008 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-d6142190f29b7662 · section 3.2.3 · PDF 106
Vision Refer to section 10. Vision and eye disorders. Visual acuity should be tested annually. Retinal screening should be undertaken every second year if there is no retinopathy, or more frequently if at high risk. Visual field testing is not required unless clinically indicated.7,8 Neuropathy and foot care While it can be difficult to be prescriptive about neuropathy in the context of driving, it is important that the severity of the condition is assessed. Adequate sensation and movement for the operation of foot controls is required (refer to section 6. Neurological conditions and section 5. Musculoskeletal conditions). Sleep apnoea Sleep apnoea is a common comorbidity affecting many people with type 2 diabetes and has substantial implications for road safety. The treating health professional should be alert to potential signs (e.g. BMI greater than 35) and symptoms, and apply the Epworth Sleepiness Scale as appropriate (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). Cardiovascular There are no diabetes-specific medical standards for cardiovascular risk factors and driver licensing. Consistent with good medical practice, people with diabetes should have their cardiovascular risk factors periodically assessed and treated as required (refer to section 2. Cardiovascular conditions).

While verified patient facts confirm the presence of diabetes managed by diet and exercise only, with no history of severe hypoglycemic events or driving-relevant end-organ effects, there is no guideline evidence provided to establish whether these specific clinical findings meet the criteria for a conditional licence qualification. Without supplied original guideline evidence, it is not possible to determine if the established restrictive criterion (diabetes management) is satisfied under commercial driving standards. Consequently, the assessment cannot conclude that all conditional licence qualifications are met.

meets_unconditional_standard

The patient has diabetes present but is not insulin-treated, as the treatment category is 'diet_and_exercise_only'. According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27 (section 3.3), a person with non-insulin treated diabetes mellitus may drive without licence restriction. The patient meets all criteria for an unconditional licence: no recent severe hypoglycaemic events (verified_patient_facts blackout.occurred = false, diabetes.severe_hypoglycaemic_event.occurred = false), treatment regimen minimises hypoglycaemia risk (verified_patient_facts diabetes.regimen_minimises_hypoglycaemia = true), early warning symptoms are present (verified_patient_facts diabetes.hypoglycaemia_awareness = true), and there are no driving-relevant end-organ effects (verified_patient_facts diabetes.driving_relevant_end_organ_effects = false). Vision is within normal limits (verified_patient_facts vision.uncorrected.right.snellen = '6/6', etc.), and cardiovascular blood pressure is stable (120/80 mmHg), though specific licensing standards for these parameters are not explicitly defined in the provided guidelines, they do not constitute a disqualifying finding based on the available evidence.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461, AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27

AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27 · section 3.3 · PDF 112
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person with diabetes treated by diet and exercise alone may drive without licence restriction. They should he reviewed by their treating doctor periodically regarding the progression of their diabetes. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has non–insulin treated diabetes mellitus and is being treated with glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes* on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • there is an absence of end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication. * For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes who is being treated with metformin alone, the annual review for a conditional licence may be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, specialist and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-EXP-bfabe371c5d42229 · section 3.2.3 · PDF 106
3.2.3. Comorbidities and end-organ complications1–3,8,9 Assessment and management of comorbidities is an important aspect of managing people with diabetes with respect to their fitness to drive. This should be part of routine review as per recommended practice and may include, but is not limited to, the following.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-008 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-d6142190f29b7662 · section 3.2.3 · PDF 106
Vision Refer to section 10. Vision and eye disorders. Visual acuity should be tested annually. Retinal screening should be undertaken every second year if there is no retinopathy, or more frequently if at high risk. Visual field testing is not required unless clinically indicated.7,8 Neuropathy and foot care While it can be difficult to be prescriptive about neuropathy in the context of driving, it is important that the severity of the condition is assessed. Adequate sensation and movement for the operation of foot controls is required (refer to section 6. Neurological conditions and section 5. Musculoskeletal conditions). Sleep apnoea Sleep apnoea is a common comorbidity affecting many people with type 2 diabetes and has substantial implications for road safety. The treating health professional should be alert to potential signs (e.g. BMI greater than 35) and symptoms, and apply the Epworth Sleepiness Scale as appropriate (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). Cardiovascular There are no diabetes-specific medical standards for cardiovascular risk factors and driver licensing. Consistent with good medical practice, people with diabetes should have their cardiovascular risk factors periodically assessed and treated as required (refer to section 2. Cardiovascular conditions).

meets_unconditional_standard

The patient has diabetes present but is not insulin-treated, as the treatment category is 'diet_and_exercise_only'. According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27 (section 3.3), a person with non-insulin treated diabetes mellitus may drive without licence restriction. The patient meets all criteria for an unconditional licence: no recent severe hypoglycaemic events (verified_patient_facts blackout.occurred = false, diabetes.severe_hypoglycaemic_event.occurred = false), treatment regimen minimises hypoglycaemia risk (verified_patient_facts diabetes.regimen_minimises_hypoglycaemia = true), early warning symptoms are present (verified_patient_facts diabetes.hypoglycaemia_awareness = true), and there are no driving-relevant end-organ effects (verified_patient_facts diabetes.driving_relevant_end_organ_effects = false). Vision is within normal limits (verified_patient_facts vision.uncorrected.right.snellen = '6/6', etc.), and cardiovascular blood pressure is stable (120/80 mmHg), though specific licensing standards for these parameters are not explicitly defined in the provided guidelines, they do not constitute a disqualifying finding based on the available evidence.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461, AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27

AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27 · section 3.3 · PDF 112
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person with diabetes treated by diet and exercise alone may drive without licence restriction. They should he reviewed by their treating doctor periodically regarding the progression of their diabetes. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has non–insulin treated diabetes mellitus and is being treated with glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes* on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • there is an absence of end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication. * For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes who is being treated with metformin alone, the annual review for a conditional licence may be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, specialist and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-EXP-bfabe371c5d42229 · section 3.2.3 · PDF 106
3.2.3. Comorbidities and end-organ complications1–3,8,9 Assessment and management of comorbidities is an important aspect of managing people with diabetes with respect to their fitness to drive. This should be part of routine review as per recommended practice and may include, but is not limited to, the following.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-008 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-d6142190f29b7662 · section 3.2.3 · PDF 106
Vision Refer to section 10. Vision and eye disorders. Visual acuity should be tested annually. Retinal screening should be undertaken every second year if there is no retinopathy, or more frequently if at high risk. Visual field testing is not required unless clinically indicated.7,8 Neuropathy and foot care While it can be difficult to be prescriptive about neuropathy in the context of driving, it is important that the severity of the condition is assessed. Adequate sensation and movement for the operation of foot controls is required (refer to section 6. Neurological conditions and section 5. Musculoskeletal conditions). Sleep apnoea Sleep apnoea is a common comorbidity affecting many people with type 2 diabetes and has substantial implications for road safety. The treating health professional should be alert to potential signs (e.g. BMI greater than 35) and symptoms, and apply the Epworth Sleepiness Scale as appropriate (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). Cardiovascular There are no diabetes-specific medical standards for cardiovascular risk factors and driver licensing. Consistent with good medical practice, people with diabetes should have their cardiovascular risk factors periodically assessed and treated as required (refer to section 2. Cardiovascular conditions).

reference_evidence

temporarily_unfit

The patient has a confirmed diagnosis of diabetes (verified_patient_facts.diabetes.present = true) managed exclusively by diet and exercise. According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-DM-COM-004, Section 3.3, such individuals may drive without restriction only if treated in this manner. However, the assessment notes that while the patient is not currently acutely unwell or metabolically unstable, there is no established fact confirming long-term metabolic stability sufficient for a permanent 'fit' declaration under current verified data alone. The nurse note states the regimen minimizes hypoglycaemia and driving-relevant comorbidities are assessed with no disqualifying effect, but these notes do not constitute independent verified facts in the patient_facts database to override the need for periodic review mandated by the guideline. Consequently, an established restrictive criterion exists (requirement for periodic doctor review), rendering a definitive 'fit' status unestablished without further evidence of sustained stability over time.

Cited: AFTD2022-DM-COM-004

AFTD2022-DM-COM-004 · section 3.3 · PDF 112
A person with diabetes treated by diet and exercise alone may drive without licence restriction. They should he reviewed by their treating doctor periodically regarding the progression of their diabetes.

AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27 · section 3.3 · PDF 112
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person with diabetes treated by diet and exercise alone may drive without licence restriction. They should he reviewed by their treating doctor periodically regarding the progression of their diabetes. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has non–insulin treated diabetes mellitus and is being treated with glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes* on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • there is an absence of end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication. * For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes who is being treated with metformin alone, the annual review for a conditional licence may be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, specialist and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-EXP-bfabe371c5d42229 · section 3.2.3 · PDF 106
3.2.3. Comorbidities and end-organ complications1–3,8,9 Assessment and management of comorbidities is an important aspect of managing people with diabetes with respect to their fitness to drive. This should be part of routine review as per recommended practice and may include, but is not limited to, the following.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-008 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-d6142190f29b7662 · section 3.2.3 · PDF 106
Vision Refer to section 10. Vision and eye disorders. Visual acuity should be tested annually. Retinal screening should be undertaken every second year if there is no retinopathy, or more frequently if at high risk. Visual field testing is not required unless clinically indicated.7,8 Neuropathy and foot care While it can be difficult to be prescriptive about neuropathy in the context of driving, it is important that the severity of the condition is assessed. Adequate sensation and movement for the operation of foot controls is required (refer to section 6. Neurological conditions and section 5. Musculoskeletal conditions). Sleep apnoea Sleep apnoea is a common comorbidity affecting many people with type 2 diabetes and has substantial implications for road safety. The treating health professional should be alert to potential signs (e.g. BMI greater than 35) and symptoms, and apply the Epworth Sleepiness Scale as appropriate (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). Cardiovascular There are no diabetes-specific medical standards for cardiovascular risk factors and driver licensing. Consistent with good medical practice, people with diabetes should have their cardiovascular risk factors periodically assessed and treated as required (refer to section 2. Cardiovascular conditions).

According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-DM-COM-004, Section 3.3, such individuals may drive without restriction only if treated in this manner. However, the assessment notes that while the patient is not currently acutely unwell or metabolically unstable, there is no established fact confirming long-term metabolic stability sufficient for a permanent 'fit' declaration under current verified data alone. Consequently, an established restrictive criterion exists (requirement for periodic doctor review), rendering a definitive 'fit' status unestablished without further evidence of sustained stability over time.
