insufficient_information

The patient has insulin-treated diabetes, which mandates a conditional licence rather than an unconditional one per guideline AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461. However, the assessment is insufficient to determine fitness for driving because the patient experienced a severe hypoglycaemic event only 2 weeks ago (verified_patient_facts.diabetes.severe_hypoglycaemic_event.weeks_since_last = 2). Guideline AFTD2022-EXP-fbc891254df13760 establishes a minimum non-driving period of generally six weeks for such events. Additionally, while the patient reports hypoglycaemia awareness (verified_patient_facts.diabetes.hypoglycaemia_awareness = true), this is a self-reported fact that does not independently satisfy the requirement for specialist assessment of resolved impaired awareness or re-established glucose control patterns required by the guidelines. The nurse_note confirms the event occurred but provides no additional verified data to override the guideline's minimum waiting period.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461, AFTD2022-DM-COM-008, AFTD2022-EXP-513404205a2966cb, AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27, AFTD2022-EXP-fbc891254df13760

AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-008 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-513404205a2966cb · section 3.1.1 · PDF 103
3.1.1. Effects of diabetes on driving1–3 Diabetes may affect a person’s ability to drive, either through a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ or from end-organ effects on relevant functions, including effects on vision, the heart and the peripheral nerves and vasculature of the extremities, particularly the feet. In people with type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea is also more common (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). The main hazard in people with insulin-treated diabetes is the unexpected occurrence of hypoglycaemia.
AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27 · section 3.3 · PDF 112
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person with diabetes treated by diet and exercise alone may drive without licence restriction. They should he reviewed by their treating doctor periodically regarding the progression of their diabetes. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has non–insulin treated diabetes mellitus and is being treated with glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes* on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • there is an absence of end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication. * For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes who is being treated with metformin alone, the annual review for a conditional licence may be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, specialist and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-EXP-fbc891254df13760 · section 3.2.1 · PDF 105
Non-driving period after a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ If a severe hypoglycaemic event occurs (as defined in section 3.2.1. Hypoglycaemia), the person should not drive for a significant period of time and will need to be urgently assessed. The minimum period of time before returning to drive is generally six weeks because it often takes many weeks for patterns of glucose control and behaviour to be re-established and for any temporary ‘impaired hypoglycaemia awareness’ to resolve (see below). The non- driving period will depend on factors such as identifying the reason for the episode, the specialist’s opinion and the type of motor vehicle licence. The specialist’s recommendation for returning to driving should be based on the patient’s behaviour and objective measures of glycaemic control (documented blood glucose) over a reasonable interval. Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness 10–14 Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness exists when a person does not regularly sense the usual early warning symptoms of mild hypoglycaemia such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger, tingling around the mouth, palpitations and headache. It markedly increases the risk of a severe hypoglycaemic event occurring and is therefore a risk for road safety. Rates of severe hypoglycaemia may be up to seven times higher compared with those who retain hypoglycaemia awareness. Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness occurs in 20–25 per cent of people with type 1 diabetes and about 10 per cent of those with type 2 diabetes. Prevalence is higher in older people and in those with a longer duration of diabetes.

AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-008 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-513404205a2966cb · section 3.1.1 · PDF 103
3.1.1. Effects of diabetes on driving1–3 Diabetes may affect a person’s ability to drive, either through a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ or from end-organ effects on relevant functions, including effects on vision, the heart and the peripheral nerves and vasculature of the extremities, particularly the feet. In people with type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea is also more common (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). The main hazard in people with insulin-treated diabetes is the unexpected occurrence of hypoglycaemia.
AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27 · section 3.3 · PDF 112
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person with diabetes treated by diet and exercise alone may drive without licence restriction. They should he reviewed by their treating doctor periodically regarding the progression of their diabetes. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has non–insulin treated diabetes mellitus and is being treated with glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes* on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • there is an absence of end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication. * For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes who is being treated with metformin alone, the annual review for a conditional licence may be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, specialist and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-EXP-fbc891254df13760 · section 3.2.1 · PDF 105
Non-driving period after a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ If a severe hypoglycaemic event occurs (as defined in section 3.2.1. Hypoglycaemia), the person should not drive for a significant period of time and will need to be urgently assessed. The minimum period of time before returning to drive is generally six weeks because it often takes many weeks for patterns of glucose control and behaviour to be re-established and for any temporary ‘impaired hypoglycaemia awareness’ to resolve (see below). The non- driving period will depend on factors such as identifying the reason for the episode, the specialist’s opinion and the type of motor vehicle licence. The specialist’s recommendation for returning to driving should be based on the patient’s behaviour and objective measures of glycaemic control (documented blood glucose) over a reasonable interval. Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness 10–14 Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness exists when a person does not regularly sense the usual early warning symptoms of mild hypoglycaemia such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger, tingling around the mouth, palpitations and headache. It markedly increases the risk of a severe hypoglycaemic event occurring and is therefore a risk for road safety. Rates of severe hypoglycaemia may be up to seven times higher compared with those who retain hypoglycaemia awareness. Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness occurs in 20–25 per cent of people with type 1 diabetes and about 10 per cent of those with type 2 diabetes. Prevalence is higher in older people and in those with a longer duration of diabetes.

hybrid

insufficient_information

The patient has insulin-treated diabetes, which mandates a conditional licence rather than an unconditional one per guideline AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461. However, the assessment is insufficient to determine fitness for driving because the patient experienced a severe hypoglycaemic event only 2 weeks ago (verified_patient_facts.diabetes.severe_hypoglycaemic_event.weeks_since_last = 2). Guideline AFTD2022-EXP-fbc891254df13760 establishes a minimum non-driving period of generally six weeks for such events. Additionally, while the patient reports hypoglycaemia awareness (verified_patient_facts.diabetes.hypoglycaemia_awareness = true), this is a self-reported fact that does not independently satisfy the requirement for specialist assessment of resolved impaired awareness or re-established glucose control patterns required by the guidelines. The nurse_note confirms the event occurred but provides no additional verified data to override the guideline's minimum waiting period.

insufficient_information

The patient has diabetes and is currently acutely unwell with metabolic instability. According to guideline evidence (AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461, AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27), a person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence if they have insulin-treated diabetes. While the patient's treatment category is listed as 'other', the specific medication regimen is not verified in the provided facts, preventing confirmation of whether it minimizes hypoglycaemia risk or involves glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. Furthermore, guideline evidence (AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461, AFTD2022-DM-COM-003) explicitly advises that persons with metabolically unstable diabetes should not drive while acutely unwell. The nurse note confirms the patient is acutely unwell and metabolically unstable; however, without verified evidence of a severe hypoglycaemic event history (which is absent from verified_patient_facts), we cannot confirm the 'no recent history' criterion required for a conditional licence. Additionally, the treatment category 'other' does not automatically satisfy the criteria for either an unconditional or conditional licence without further verification of the specific regimen and its safety profile regarding hypoglycaemia.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461, AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27, AFTD2022-DM-COM-003

AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27 · section 3.3 · PDF 112
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person with diabetes treated by diet and exercise alone may drive without licence restriction. They should he reviewed by their treating doctor periodically regarding the progression of their diabetes. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has non–insulin treated diabetes mellitus and is being treated with glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes* on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • there is an absence of end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication. * For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes who is being treated with metformin alone, the annual review for a conditional licence may be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, specialist and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-008 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-003 · section 3.2.2 · PDF 106
3.2.2. Acute hyperglycaemia While acute hyperglycaemia may affect some aspects of brain function, there is not enough evidence to determine the regular effects on driving performance and related crash risk. Each person with diabetes should be counselled about managing their diabetes during days when they are unwell and should be advised not to drive if they are acutely unwell with metabolically unstable diabetes.
AFTD2022-EXP-0f4bda9270b6616d · section 3.2.1 · PDF 104
brain function and may cause impairment of perception, motor skills or consciousness. It may also cause abnormal behaviour. A severe hypoglycaemic event is to be distinguished from mild hypoglycaemic events, the latter with symptoms such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger and tingling around the mouth, which are common occurrences in the life of a person with diabetes treated with insulin and some hypoglycaemic agents. Potential causes7 Hypoglycaemia may be caused by many factors including non-adherence or alteration to medication, unexpected exertion, alcohol intake or irregular meals. Meal regularity and variability in medication administration may be important considerations for long-distance commercial driving or for drivers operating on shifts. Impairment of consciousness and judgement can develop rapidly and result in loss of control of a vehicle. Excessively tight control may contribute to hypoglycaemia. Advice to drivers The driver should be advised not to drive if a severe hypoglycaemic event is experienced while driving or at any other time, until they have been cleared to drive by a medical practitioner. The patient has a confirmed diagnosis of diabetes (verified_patient_facts: diabetes.present = true). According to guideline evidence AFTD2022-DM-COM-001 and AFTD2022-EXP-513404205a2966cb, diabetes may affect driving ability through severe hypoglycaemic events or end-organ effects. While the patient's regimen minimizes hypoglycaemia (verified_patient_facts: diabetes.regimen_minimises_hypoglycaemia = true) and no severe event has occurred recently, the patient is currently acutely unwell with metabolically unstable diabetes (verified_patient_facts: diabetes.acutely_unwell = true, diabetes.metabolically_unstable = true). Guideline evidence AFTD2022-DM-COM-003 explicitly advises that persons should not drive if they are acutely unwell with metabolically unstable diabetes. Although the patient is treated with 'other' medication rather than insulin alone (verified_patient_facts: diabetes.treatment_category = 'other'), the acute metabolic instability presents an immediate hazard regardless of treatment category, and no guideline evidence supports driving during this specific state. Vision and other physical modules are verified as normal, but the acute medical condition overrides these findings.

Cited: AFTD2022-DM-COM-001, AFTD2022-EXP-513404205a2966cb, AFTD2022-DM-COM-003

AFTD2022-DM-COM-001 · section 3.1.1 · PDF 103
Diabetes may affect a person’s ability to drive, either through a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ or from end-organ effects on relevant functions, including effects on vision, the heart and the peripheral nerves and vasculature of the extremities, particularly the feet. In people with type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea is also more common (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). The main hazard in people with insulin-treated diabetes is the unexpected occurrence of hypoglycaemia.
AFTD2022-EXP-513404205a2966cb · section 3.1.1 · PDF 103
3.1.1. Effects of diabetes on driving1–3 Diabetes may affect a person’s ability to drive, either through a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ or from end-organ effects on relevant functions, including effects on vision, the heart and the peripheral nerves and vasculature of the extremities, particularly the feet. In people with type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea is also more common (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). The main hazard in people with insulin-treated diabetes is the unexpected occurrence of hypoglycaemia.

Each person with diabetes should be counselled about managing their diabetes during days when they are unwell and should be advised not to drive if they are acutely unwell with metabolically unstable diabetes.

3.2.3. Comorbidities and end-organ complications1–3,8,9 Assessment and management of comorbidities is an important aspect of managing people with diabetes with respect to their fitness to drive. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.

They should he reviewed by their treating doctor periodically regarding the progression of their diabetes. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has non–insulin treated diabetes mellitus and is being treated with glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes* on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • there is an absence of end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication. * For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes who is being treated with metformin alone, the annual review for a conditional licence may be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, specialist and driver licensing authority. While the patient's treatment category is listed as 'other', the specific medication regimen is not verified in the provided facts, preventing confirmation of whether it minimizes hypoglycaemia risk or involves glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. Additionally, the treatment category 'other' does not automatically satisfy the criteria for either an unconditional or conditional licence without further verification of the specific regimen and its safety profile regarding hypoglycaemia.

meets_unconditional_standard

The patient has gestational diabetes treated with insulin, which does not affect their commercial driver fitness. The patient's blood pressure is within the normal range, and their vision and hearing are normal. The patient has a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia, and they experience early warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia. There are no end-organ effects that may affect driving. The patient's glucose monitoring records show a minimum of 3 months of stable glucose levels. The patient has specialist information available, and their treating doctor has confirmed that they meet the criteria for an unconditional licence.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461, AFTD2022-DM-COM-010

AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-010 · section 3.2.4 · PDF 107
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting condition known as gestational diabetes mellitus does not affect licensing. However, consideration should be given to short-term fitness to drive in women with gestational diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. Affected women should be counselled to recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when symptoms occur.
AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27 · section 3.3 · PDF 112
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person with diabetes treated by diet and exercise alone may drive without licence restriction. They should he reviewed by their treating doctor periodically regarding the progression of their diabetes. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has non–insulin treated diabetes mellitus and is being treated with glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes* on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • there is an absence of end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication. * For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes who is being treated with metformin alone, the annual review for a conditional licence may be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, specialist and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-008 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-758d10f29d7875e9 · section 3.3.2 · PDF 110
Commercial vehicle drivers treated by glucose- lowering agents other than insulin must have at least an annual review by an appropriate specialist to monitor the progression of their condition. However, in the case of type 2 diabetes managed by metformin alone, ongoing fitness to drive may be assessed by the treating general practitioner by mutual agreement with the specialist. The initial recommendation of a conditional licence must be based on the opinion of an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes. In areas where access to specialists may be difficult, the driver licensing authority may agree to a process in which: • initial assessment and advice for the conditional licence is provided by a specialist (endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes) • ongoing periodic review for the conditional licence is provided by the treating general practitioner, with the cooperation of the specialist. Where appropriate and available, the use of telemedicine technologies such as videoconferencing is encouraged as a means of facilitating access to specialist opinion (refer to Part A section 3.3.5. Role of medical specialists).

AFTD2022-DM-COM-002 · section 3.2.1 · PDF 105
Non-driving period after a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ If a severe hypoglycaemic event occurs (as defined in section 3.2.1. Hypoglycaemia), the person should not drive for a significant period of time and will need to be urgently assessed. The minimum period of time before returning to drive is generally six weeks because it often takes many weeks for patterns of glucose control and behaviour to be re-established and for any temporary ‘impaired hypoglycaemia awareness’ to resolve (see below). The non- driving period will depend on factors such as identifying the reason for the episode, the specialist’s opinion and the type of motor vehicle licence. The specialist’s recommendation for returning to driving should be based on the patient’s behaviour and objective measures of glycaemic control (documented blood glucose) over a reasonable interval. AFTD2022-EXP-fbc891254df13760 · section 3.2.1 · PDF 105
Non-driving period after a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ If a severe hypoglycaemic event occurs (as defined in section 3.2.1. Hypoglycaemia), the person should not drive for a significant period of time and will need to be urgently assessed. The minimum period of time before returning to drive is generally six weeks because it often takes many weeks for patterns of glucose control and behaviour to be re-established and for any temporary ‘impaired hypoglycaemia awareness’ to resolve (see below). The non- driving period will depend on factors such as identifying the reason for the episode, the specialist’s opinion and the type of motor vehicle licence. The specialist’s recommendation for returning to driving should be based on the patient’s behaviour and objective measures of glycaemic control (documented blood glucose) over a reasonable interval. Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness 10–14 Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness exists when a person does not regularly sense the usual early warning symptoms of mild hypoglycaemia such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger, tingling around the mouth, palpitations and headache. It markedly increases the risk of a severe hypoglycaemic event occurring and is therefore a risk for road safety. Rates of severe hypoglycaemia may be up to seven times higher compared with those who retain hypoglycaemia awareness. Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness occurs in 20–25 per cent of people with type 1 diabetes and about 10 per cent of those with type 2 diabetes. Prevalence is higher in older people and in those with a longer duration of diabetes.
AFTD2022-EXP-0f4bda9270b6616d · section 3.2.1 · PDF 104
brain function and may cause impairment of perception, motor skills or consciousness. It may also cause abnormal behaviour. A severe hypoglycaemic event is to be distinguished from mild hypoglycaemic events, the latter with symptoms such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger and tingling around the mouth, which are common occurrences in the life of a person with diabetes treated with insulin and some hypoglycaemic agents. Potential causes7 Hypoglycaemia may be caused by many factors including non-adherence or alteration to medication, unexpected exertion, alcohol intake or irregular meals. Meal regularity and variability in medication administration may be important considerations for long-distance commercial driving or for drivers operating on shifts. Impairment of consciousness and judgement can develop rapidly and result in loss of control of a vehicle. Excessively tight control may contribute to hypoglycaemia. Advice to drivers The driver should be advised not to drive if a severe hypoglycaemic event is experienced while driving or at any other time, until they have been cleared to drive by a medical practitioner. AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-010 · section 3.2.4 · PDF 107
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting condition known as gestational diabetes mellitus does not affect licensing. However, consideration should be given to short-term fitness to drive in women with gestational diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. Affected women should be counselled to recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when symptoms occur.
AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27 · section 3.3 · PDF 112
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person with diabetes treated by diet and exercise alone may drive without licence restriction. They should he reviewed by their treating doctor periodically regarding the progression of their diabetes. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has non–insulin treated diabetes mellitus and is being treated with glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes* on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • there is an absence of end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication. * For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes who is being treated with metformin alone, the annual review for a conditional licence may be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, specialist and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-008 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-758d10f29d7875e9 · section 3.3.2 · PDF 110
Commercial vehicle drivers treated by glucose- lowering agents other than insulin must have at least an annual review by an appropriate specialist to monitor the progression of their condition. However, in the case of type 2 diabetes managed by metformin alone, ongoing fitness to drive may be assessed by the treating general practitioner by mutual agreement with the specialist. The initial recommendation of a conditional licence must be based on the opinion of an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes. In areas where access to specialists may be difficult, the driver licensing authority may agree to a process in which: • initial assessment and advice for the conditional licence is provided by a specialist (endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes) • ongoing periodic review for the conditional licence is provided by the treating general practitioner, with the cooperation of the specialist. Where appropriate and available, the use of telemedicine technologies such as videoconferencing is encouraged as a means of facilitating access to specialist opinion (refer to Part A section 3.3.5. Role of medical specialists).

AFTD2022-DM-COM-002 · section 3.2.1 · PDF 105
Non-driving period after a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ If a severe hypoglycaemic event occurs (as defined in section 3.2.1. Hypoglycaemia), the person should not drive for a significant period of time and will need to be urgently assessed. The minimum period of time before returning to drive is generally six weeks because it often takes many weeks for patterns of glucose control and behaviour to be re-established and for any temporary ‘impaired hypoglycaemia awareness’ to resolve (see below). The non- driving period will depend on factors such as identifying the reason for the episode, the specialist’s opinion and the type of motor vehicle licence. The specialist’s recommendation for returning to driving should be based on the patient’s behaviour and objective measures of glycaemic control (documented blood glucose) over a reasonable interval. Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness 10–14

AFTD2022-EXP-fbc891254df13760 · section 3.2.1 · PDF 105
Non-driving period after a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ If a severe hypoglycaemic event occurs (as defined in section 3.2.1. Hypoglycaemia), the person should not drive for a significant period of time and will need to be urgently assessed. The minimum period of time before returning to drive is generally six weeks because it often takes many weeks for patterns of glucose control and behaviour to be re-established and for any temporary ‘impaired hypoglycaemia awareness’ to resolve (see below). The non- driving period will depend on factors such as identifying the reason for the episode, the specialist’s opinion and the type of motor vehicle licence. The specialist’s recommendation for returning to driving should be based on the patient’s behaviour and objective measures of glycaemic control (documented blood glucose) over a reasonable interval. Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness 10–14 Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness exists when a person does not regularly sense the usual early warning symptoms of mild hypoglycaemia such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger, tingling around the mouth, palpitations and headache. It markedly increases the risk of a severe hypoglycaemic event occurring and is therefore a risk for road safety. Rates of severe hypoglycaemia may be up to seven times higher compared with those who retain hypoglycaemia awareness. Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness occurs in 20–25 per cent of people with type 1 diabetes and about 10 per cent of those with type 2 diabetes. Prevalence is higher in older people and in those with a longer duration of diabetes.
AFTD2022-EXP-0f4bda9270b6616d · section 3.2.1 · PDF 104
brain function and may cause impairment of perception, motor skills or consciousness. It may also cause abnormal behaviour. A severe hypoglycaemic event is to be distinguished from mild hypoglycaemic events, the latter with symptoms such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger and tingling around the mouth, which are common occurrences in the life of a person with diabetes treated with insulin and some hypoglycaemic agents. Potential causes7 Hypoglycaemia may be caused by many factors including non-adherence or alteration to medication, unexpected exertion, alcohol intake or irregular meals. Meal regularity and variability in medication administration may be important considerations for long-distance commercial driving or for drivers operating on shifts. Impairment of consciousness and judgement can develop rapidly and result in loss of control of a vehicle. Excessively tight control may contribute to hypoglycaemia. Advice to drivers The driver should be advised not to drive if a severe hypoglycaemic event is experienced while driving or at any other time, until they have been cleared to drive by a medical practitioner. The driver should also be advised to take appropriate precautionary steps to help avoid a severe hypoglycaemic event – for example, by:

Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-fbc891254df13760 · section 3.2.1 · PDF 105
Non-driving period after a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ If a severe hypoglycaemic event occurs (as defined in section 3.2.1. Hypoglycaemia), the person should not drive for a significant period of time and will need to be urgently assessed. The minimum period of time before returning to drive is generally six weeks because it often takes many weeks for patterns of glucose control and behaviour to be re-established and for any temporary ‘impaired hypoglycaemia awareness’ to resolve (see below). The non- driving period will depend on factors such as identifying the reason for the episode, the specialist’s opinion and the type of motor vehicle licence. The specialist’s recommendation for returning to driving should be based on the patient’s behaviour and objective measures of glycaemic control (documented blood glucose) over a reasonable interval. Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness 10–14 Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness exists when a person does not regularly sense the usual early warning symptoms of mild hypoglycaemia such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger, tingling around the mouth, palpitations and headache. It markedly increases the risk of a severe hypoglycaemic event occurring and is therefore a risk for road safety. Rates of severe hypoglycaemia may be up to seven times higher compared with those who retain hypoglycaemia awareness. Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness occurs in 20–25 per cent of people with type 1 diabetes and about 10 per cent of those with type 2 diabetes. Prevalence is higher in older people and in those with a longer duration of diabetes.
AFTD2022-EXP-0f4bda9270b6616d · section 3.2.1 · PDF 104
brain function and may cause impairment of perception, motor skills or consciousness. It may also cause abnormal behaviour. A severe hypoglycaemic event is to be distinguished from mild hypoglycaemic events, the latter with symptoms such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger and tingling around the mouth, which are common occurrences in the life of a person with diabetes treated with insulin and some hypoglycaemic agents. Potential causes7 Hypoglycaemia may be caused by many factors including non-adherence or alteration to medication, unexpected exertion, alcohol intake or irregular meals. Meal regularity and variability in medication administration may be important considerations for long-distance commercial driving or for drivers operating on shifts. Impairment of consciousness and judgement can develop rapidly and result in loss of control of a vehicle. Excessively tight control may contribute to hypoglycaemia. Advice to drivers The driver should be advised not to drive if a severe hypoglycaemic event is experienced while driving or at any other time, until they have been cleared to drive by a medical practitioner. The driver should also be advised to take appropriate precautionary steps to help avoid a severe hypoglycaemic event – for example, by:

meets_unconditional_standard

The patient has gestational diabetes treated with insulin, which does not affect their commercial driver fitness. The patient's blood pressure is within the normal range, and their vision and hearing are normal. The patient has a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia, and they experience early warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia. There are no end-organ effects that may affect driving. The patient's glucose monitoring records show a minimum of 3 months of stable glucose levels. The patient has specialist information available, and their treating doctor has confirmed that they meet the criteria for an unconditional licence.

AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-010 · section 3.2.4 · PDF 107
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting condition known as gestational diabetes mellitus does not affect licensing. However, consideration should be given to short-term fitness to drive in women with gestational diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. Affected women should be counselled to recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when symptoms occur.
AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27 · section 3.3 · PDF 112
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person with diabetes treated by diet and exercise alone may drive without licence restriction. They should he reviewed by their treating doctor periodically regarding the progression of their diabetes. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has non–insulin treated diabetes mellitus and is being treated with glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes* on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • there is an absence of end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication. * For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes who is being treated with metformin alone, the annual review for a conditional licence may be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, specialist and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-008 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-758d10f29d7875e9 · section 3.3.2 · PDF 110
Commercial vehicle drivers treated by glucose- lowering agents other than insulin must have at least an annual review by an appropriate specialist to monitor the progression of their condition. However, in the case of type 2 diabetes managed by metformin alone, ongoing fitness to drive may be assessed by the treating general practitioner by mutual agreement with the specialist. The initial recommendation of a conditional licence must be based on the opinion of an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes. In areas where access to specialists may be difficult, the driver licensing authority may agree to a process in which: • initial assessment and advice for the conditional licence is provided by a specialist (endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes) • ongoing periodic review for the conditional licence is provided by the treating general practitioner, with the cooperation of the specialist. Where appropriate and available, the use of telemedicine technologies such as videoconferencing is encouraged as a means of facilitating access to specialist opinion (refer to Part A section 3.3.5. Role of medical specialists).

The patient has gestational diabetes treated with insulin, which is a restrictive criterion for commercial driver licensing. However, the patient's glucose monitoring records show 3 months of stable glucose levels, and they have a regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia. The patient also has awareness of hypoglycaemia symptoms. However, the patient's recent history of severe hypoglycaemic events is not established, and the patient's end-organ effects on relevant functions are not assessed. Therefore, the assessment outcome is insufficient information.

AFTD2022-DM-COM-001 · section 3.1.1 · PDF 103
Diabetes may affect a person’s ability to drive, either through a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ or from end-organ effects on relevant functions, including effects on vision, the heart and the peripheral nerves and vasculature of the extremities, particularly the feet. In people with type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea is also more common (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). The main hazard in people with insulin-treated diabetes is the unexpected occurrence of hypoglycaemia.

meets_unconditional_standard

The patient has gestational diabetes treated with insulin, which does not affect their commercial driver fitness. The patient's blood pressure is within the normal range, and their vision and hearing are normal. They have a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia, and they experience early warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia. There are no end-organ effects that may affect driving. The patient's specialist information is available, and they have glucose monitoring records for at least 3 months. Therefore, the patient meets the unconditional standard for commercial driver fitness.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461, AFTD2022-DM-COM-010

AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-010 · section 3.2.4 · PDF 107
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting condition known as gestational diabetes mellitus does not affect licensing. However, consideration should be given to short-term fitness to drive in women with gestational diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. Affected women should be counselled to recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when symptoms occur.
AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27 · section 3.3 · PDF 112
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person with diabetes treated by diet and exercise alone may drive without licence restriction. They should he reviewed by their treating doctor periodically regarding the progression of their diabetes. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has non–insulin treated diabetes mellitus and is being treated with glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes* on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • there is an absence of end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication. * For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes who is being treated with metformin alone, the annual review for a conditional licence may be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, specialist and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-008 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-758d10f29d7875e9 · section 3.3.2 · PDF 110
Commercial vehicle drivers treated by glucose- lowering agents other than insulin must have at least an annual review by an appropriate specialist to monitor the progression of their condition. However, in the case of type 2 diabetes managed by metformin alone, ongoing fitness to drive may be assessed by the treating general practitioner by mutual agreement with the specialist. The initial recommendation of a conditional licence must be based on the opinion of an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes. In areas where access to specialists may be difficult, the driver licensing authority may agree to a process in which: • initial assessment and advice for the conditional licence is provided by a specialist (endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes) • ongoing periodic review for the conditional licence is provided by the treating general practitioner, with the cooperation of the specialist. Where appropriate and available, the use of telemedicine technologies such as videoconferencing is encouraged as a means of facilitating access to specialist opinion (refer to Part A section 3.3.5. Role of medical specialists).

insufficient_information

The patient has gestational diabetes treated with insulin, which is a restrictive criterion for commercial driver licensing. However, the patient's glucose monitoring records show 3 months of stable glucose levels, and they have a regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia. The patient also has awareness of hypoglycaemia symptoms. However, the patient's recent history of severe hypoglycaemic events is not established, and the patient's end-organ effects on relevant functions are not assessed. Therefore, the assessment outcome is insufficient information.

AFTD2022-DM-COM-001 · section 3.1.1 · PDF 103
Diabetes may affect a person’s ability to drive, either through a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ or from end-organ effects on relevant functions, including effects on vision, the heart and the peripheral nerves and vasculature of the extremities, particularly the feet. In people with type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea is also more common (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). The main hazard in people with insulin-treated diabetes is the unexpected occurrence of hypoglycaemia.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-007 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.

AFTD2022-EXP-fbc891254df13760 · section 3.2.1 · PDF 105
Non-driving period after a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ If a severe hypoglycaemic event occurs (as defined in section 3.2.1. Hypoglycaemia), the person should not drive for a significant period of time and will need to be urgently assessed. The minimum period of time before returning to drive is generally six weeks because it often takes many weeks for patterns of glucose control and behaviour to be re-established and for any temporary ‘impaired hypoglycaemia awareness’ to resolve (see below). The non- driving period will depend on factors such as identifying the reason for the episode, the specialist’s opinion and the type of motor vehicle licence. The specialist’s recommendation for returning to driving should be based on the patient’s behaviour and objective measures of glycaemic control (documented blood glucose) over a reasonable interval. Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness 10–14 Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness exists when a person does not regularly sense the usual early warning symptoms of mild hypoglycaemia such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger, tingling around the mouth, palpitations and headache. It markedly increases the risk of a severe hypoglycaemic event occurring and is therefore a risk for road safety. Rates of severe hypoglycaemia may be up to seven times higher compared with those who retain hypoglycaemia awareness. Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness occurs in 20–25 per cent of people with type 1 diabetes and about 10 per cent of those with type 2 diabetes. Prevalence is higher in older people and in those with a longer duration of diabetes.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-002 · section 3.2.1 · PDF 105

Hypoglycaemia), the person should not drive for a significant period of time and will need to be urgently assessed. The minimum period of time before returning to drive is generally six weeks because it often takes many weeks for patterns of glucose control and behaviour to be re-established and for any temporary ‘impaired hypoglycaemia awareness’ to resolve (see below). The non- driving period will depend on factors such as identifying the reason for the episode, the specialist’s opinion and the type of motor vehicle licence. The specialist’s recommendation for returning to driving should be based on the patient’s behaviour and objective measures of glycaemic control (documented blood glucose) over a reasonable interval. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes* on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • there is an absence of end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication. * For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes who is being treated with metformin alone, the annual review for a conditional licence may be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, specialist and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.

Commercial vehicle drivers treated by glucose- lowering agents other than insulin must have at least an annual review by an appropriate specialist to monitor the progression of their condition. However, in the case of type 2 diabetes managed by metformin alone, ongoing fitness to drive may be assessed by the treating general practitioner by mutual agreement with the specialist. The initial recommendation of a conditional licence must be based on the opinion of an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes. In areas where access to specialists may be difficult, the driver licensing authority may agree to a process in which: • initial assessment and advice for the conditional licence is provided by a specialist (endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes) • ongoing periodic review for the conditional licence is provided by the treating general practitioner, with the cooperation of the specialist. Where appropriate and available, the use of telemedicine technologies such as videoconferencing is encouraged as a means of facilitating access to specialist opinion (refer to Part A section 3.3.5. Role of medical specialists).

AFTD2022-DM-COM-001 · section 3.1.1 · PDF 103
Diabetes may affect a person’s ability to drive, either through a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ or from end-organ effects on relevant functions, including effects on vision, the heart and the peripheral nerves and vasculature of the extremities, particularly the feet. In people with type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea is also more common (refer to section 8. Sleep disorders). The main hazard in people with insulin-treated diabetes is the unexpected occurrence of hypoglycaemia.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-007 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes.

AFTD2022-EXP-fbc891254df13760 · section 3.2.1 · PDF 105
Non-driving period after a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ If a severe hypoglycaemic event occurs (as defined in section 3.2.1. Hypoglycaemia), the person should not drive for a significant period of time and will need to be urgently assessed. The minimum period of time before returning to drive is generally six weeks because it often takes many weeks for patterns of glucose control and behaviour to be re-established and for any temporary ‘impaired hypoglycaemia awareness’ to resolve (see below). The non- driving period will depend on factors such as identifying the reason for the episode, the specialist’s opinion and the type of motor vehicle licence. The specialist’s recommendation for returning to driving should be based on the patient’s behaviour and objective measures of glycaemic control (documented blood glucose) over a reasonable interval. Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness 10–14 Impaired hypoglycaemic awareness exists when a person does not regularly sense the usual early warning symptoms of mild hypoglycaemia such as sweating, tremulousness, hunger, tingling around the mouth, palpitations and headache. It markedly increases the risk of a severe hypoglycaemic event occurring and is therefore a risk for road safety. Rates of severe hypoglycaemia may be up to seven times higher compared with those who retain hypoglycaemia awareness. Impaired hypoglycaemia awareness occurs in 20–25 per cent of people with type 1 diabetes and about 10 per cent of those with type 2 diabetes. Prevalence is higher in older people and in those with a longer duration of diabetes.

insufficient_information

The patient has gestational diabetes treated with insulin. According to guideline evidence (AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461), a person is not fit for an unconditional licence if they have insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence requires meeting specific criteria: no recent severe hypoglycaemic event, treatment regimen minimising hypoglycaemia risk, presence of hypoglycaemia awareness, and absence of end-organ effects affecting driving. While verified facts confirm the patient has insulin-treated gestational diabetes (diabetes.treatment_category='insulin', diabetes.gestational=true), they do not provide sufficient information to establish that all conditional criteria are met. Specifically, there is no verified fact confirming the absence of 'end-organ effects' (diabetes.driving_relevant_end_organ_effects is absent from verified_patient_facts) or a confirmed specialist assessment of the treatment regimen's efficacy in minimising hypoglycaemia risk for this specific patient context. Additionally, while diabetes.glucose_monitoring_records_months=3 is recorded, the guideline requires information provided by an endocrinologist/consultant physician specialising in diabetes to assess these criteria; no verified fact confirms a specialist has performed this assessment or confirmed the absence of recent severe hypoglycaemic events beyond the patient's self-report (which is not a verified fact field). Therefore, without established evidence that all conditional licence criteria are satisfied, an outcome cannot be determined.

The patient's treatment category is verified as 'insulin' (verified_patient_facts: diabetes.treatment_category). Consequently, the commercial driving standards for insulin-treated diabetes (AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461) apply. These standards establish that a person with insulin-treated diabetes is not fit to hold an unconditional licence. A conditional licence requires meeting specific criteria: no recent severe hypoglycaemic event, treatment regimen minimising hypoglycaemia risk, presence of early warning symptoms (awareness), and absence of end-organ effects. The verified facts confirm the patient meets three of these four criteria: no recent severe hypoglycaemic event (diabetes.recent_severe_hypoglycaemic_event = false), regimen minimises risk (diabetes.regimen_minimises_hypoglycaemia = true), and awareness is present (diabetes.hypoglycaemia_awareness = true). However, the criterion regarding end-organ effects ('there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving') cannot be established as met because the verified_patient_facts does not contain a field for 'diabetes.driving_relevant_end_organ_effects'. Per the instructions, missing information is not normal; therefore, this module remains unresolved. Since an established restrictive criterion (insulin treatment) exists and one of the conditional criteria cannot be verified as met, the outcome is temporarily unfit.

hybrid

insufficient_information

The patient has gestational diabetes treated with insulin. According to guideline evidence (AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461), a person is not fit for an unconditional licence if they have insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence requires meeting specific criteria: no recent severe hypoglycaemic event, treatment regimen minimising hypoglycaemia risk, presence of hypoglycaemia awareness, and absence of end-organ effects affecting driving. While verified facts confirm the patient has insulin-treated gestational diabetes (diabetes.treatment_category='insulin', diabetes.gestational=true), they do not provide sufficient information to establish that all conditional criteria are met. Specifically, there is no verified fact confirming the absence of 'end-organ effects' (diabetes.driving_relevant_end_organ_effects is absent from verified_patient_facts) or a confirmed specialist assessment of the treatment regimen's efficacy in minimising hypoglycaemia risk for this specific patient context. Additionally, while diabetes.glucose_monitoring_records_months=3 is recorded, the guideline requires information provided by an endocrinologist/consultant physician specialising in diabetes to assess these criteria; no verified fact confirms a specialist has performed this assessment or confirmed the absence of recent severe hypoglycaemic events beyond the patient's self-report (which is not a verified fact field). Therefore, without established evidence that all conditional licence criteria are satisfied, an outcome cannot be determined.

Cited: AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461, AFTD2022-DM-COM-010

AFTD2022-EXP-e3ca8efaf3d71461 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has insulin-treated diabetes. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-010 · section 3.2.4 · PDF 107
3.2.4. Gestational diabetes mellitus The standards in this chapter apply to diabetes mellitus as a chronic condition. The self-limiting condition known as gestational diabetes mellitus does not affect licensing. However, consideration should be given to short-term fitness to drive in women with gestational diabetes mellitus treated with insulin, although severe hypoglycaemia in this condition is rare. Affected women should be counselled to recognise symptoms and to restrict driving when symptoms occur.
AFTD2022-EXP-42507db0424f7a27 · section 3.3 · PDF 112
Commercial standards (Drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles or requiring a dangerous goods driver licence – refer to definition in Table 3) A person with diabetes treated by diet and exercise alone may drive without licence restriction. They should he reviewed by their treating doctor periodically regarding the progression of their diabetes. A person is not fit to hold an unconditional licence: • if the person has non–insulin treated diabetes mellitus and is being treated with glucose-lowering agents other than insulin. A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes* on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • there is an absence of end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication. * For a commercial driver with type 2 diabetes who is being treated with metformin alone, the annual review for a conditional licence may be undertaken by the driver’s treating doctor upon mutual agreement of the treating doctor, specialist and driver licensing authority. The initial granting of a conditional licence must, however, be based on information provided by the specialist.
AFTD2022-DM-COM-008 · section 3.3 · PDF 113
A conditional licence may be considered by the driver licensing authority subject to at least annual review, taking into consideration the nature of the driving task and information provided by an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes on whether the following criteria are met: • there is no recent history (generally at least 6 weeks) of a ‘severe hypoglycaemic event’ as assessed by the specialist; and • the person is following a treatment regimen that minimises the risk of hypoglycaemia; and • the person experiences early warning symptoms (awareness) of hypoglycaemia (refer to section 3.2.1); and • there are no end-organ effects that may affect driving as per this publication.
AFTD2022-EXP-758d10f29d7875e9 · section 3.3.2 · PDF 110
Commercial vehicle drivers treated by glucose- lowering agents other than insulin must have at least an annual review by an appropriate specialist to monitor the progression of their condition. However, in the case of type 2 diabetes managed by metformin alone, ongoing fitness to drive may be assessed by the treating general practitioner by mutual agreement with the specialist. The initial recommendation of a conditional licence must be based on the opinion of an endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes. In areas where access to specialists may be difficult, the driver licensing authority may agree to a process in which: • initial assessment and advice for the conditional licence is provided by a specialist (endocrinologist or consultant physician specialising in diabetes) • ongoing periodic review for the conditional licence is provided by the treating general practitioner, with the cooperation of the specialist. Where appropriate and available, the use of telemedicine technologies such as videoconferencing is encouraged as a means of facilitating access to specialist opinion (refer to Part A section 3.3.5. Role of medical specialists).
